articles.title: What went wrong for TMC? How divided Muslim votes helped BJP break into key West Bengal seats
articles.snippet: BJP’s gains in Muslim-dominated seats in West Bengal are being driven less by a shift in Muslim votes and more by their division among multiple parties like Congress, ISF, and AIMIM-AJUP.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: BJP’s gains in Muslim-dominated seats in West Bengal are being driven less by a shift in Muslim votes and more by their division among multiple parties like Congress, ISF, and AIMIM-AJUP.
articles.body: The Bharatiya Janata Party is surging ahead in the West Bengal Assembly elections, leading in around 197 seats and on course to dethrone Mamata Banerjee’s Trinamool Congress. While the scale of this lead points to a broader political shift, one of the most striking patterns is emerging in constituencies with a high Muslim population.    TMC, which has traditionally relied on a consolidated Muslim vote, is losing ground in at least nine such seats, while the BJP is gaining in at least five constituencies where Muslims form over 50 per cent of the electorate. This is not because Muslim voters are shifting en masse toward the BJP. The more decisive factor is fragmentation.    Entry of multiple Muslim-centric players    One of the biggest reasons behind this shift is the crowded field of parties competing for Muslim votes. Apart from the Trinamool Congress, which has traditionally dominated these constituencies, several other players entered the fray this time. These include the Indian National Congress, the Left Front led by Communist Party of India (Marxist) in alliance with the Indian Secular Front, and the Aam Janata Unnayan Party, which aligned with Asaduddin Owaisi’s political network.    In several constituencies, these parties fielded Muslim candidates and directly competed for the same voter base that once consolidated behind the TMC. While most of them are not leading in many seats, their presence has been enough to split votes in tightly contested constituencies.    Earlier, Muslim voters often voted strategically in favour of the TMC to block the Bharatiya Janata Party. This time, that consolidation appears to have weakened, with votes getting divided across multiple parties, altering outcomes in key seats.    The arithmetic of division    In a first-past-the-post system, unity matters more than numbers. When a dominant vote bank splits across multiple parties, even a smaller but consolidated vote can win.    This is exactly what is playing out. The Muslim vote, divided between TMC, ISF, Congress, Left candidates, and others, has reduced the TMC’s winning margins. At the same time, the BJP’s relatively stable vote base has allowed it to edge ahead in close contests.    Local dissatisfaction adds to the split    There are also signs of dissatisfaction among sections of Muslim voters with the TMC. Issues such as local governance, candidate selection, and political outreach have pushed some voters to explore alternatives.    Importantly, this has not translated into support for the BJP. Instead, votes have moved toward smaller parties or independents. But the outcome remains the same. The TMC’s vote share gets diluted.    As Suvendu Adhikari put it, there has been a “bifurcation” in voting patterns.    BJP’s consolidation strategy    While the opposition vote is splitting, the BJP has focused on consolidating non-Muslim voters, especially among Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes.    This combination of division on one side and consolidation on the other has amplified the BJP’s advantage. Even in constituencies where Muslims form a majority, the party is benefiting from this electoral arithmetic.    The SIR controversy    The issue of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls has also surfaced during the election. Opposition parties have alleged that the process may have disproportionately affected Muslim voters.    However, available data suggests that exclusions were not limited to one community, with both Hindu and Muslim voters impacted. While the controversy has added to the political debate, its direct effect on results remains contested.    What this means    The BJP’s rise in Muslim-dominated seats is not the result of a dramatic shift in community voting patterns. It is the outcome of fragmentation within the opposition.    With parties like ISF and others entering the fray, the once consolidated Muslim vote bank is now divided. In tight contests, that division is enough to change results.    For the TMC, this presents a clear challenge. Rebuilding trust and consolidating support will be key. For the BJP, the current trend shows how electoral arithmetic, not just vote share, can redefine outcomes.

articles.title: Congress leader Gaurav Gogoi loses to BJP’s Hitendra Nath Goswami in Assam's Jorhat
articles.snippet: Goswami secured a total of 69,439 votes, winning by a margin of 23,182 votes over Gogoi, who polled 46,257 votes.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Goswami secured a total of 69,439 votes, winning by a margin of 23,182 votes over Gogoi, who polled 46,257 votes.
articles.body: In a key result from the Assam Assembly elections, Congress candidate Gaurav Gogoi was defeated in the Jorhat Assembly constituency by BJP leader Hitendra Nath Goswami, according to the Election Commission of India (ECI).    Goswami secured a total of 69,439 votes, winning by a margin of 23,182 votes over Gogoi, who polled 46,257 votes. The gap remained intact as the final round of counting concluded, sealing the outcome in favour of the BJP candidate.    Statewide trends pointed to a strong showing for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which appeared set to return to power with a dominant performance.    The party was leading in 79 seats, comfortably above the majority mark of 64 in the 126-member Assembly, reflecting a decisive electoral mandate.    The results underscored a significant setback for the Congress-led opposition. Despite organisational changes and efforts to regain ground, the party struggled to reconnect with several of its traditional voter bases.    Its inability to win back support among the Ahom community, tea garden tribes, and sections of Muslim voters in Upper Assam contributed to its poor performance across crucial constituencies.    As per ECI trends, the Indian National Congress was ahead in 23 seats. The Bodoland People’s Front (BPF) led in 10 seats, while the Asom Gana Parishad (AGP) was ahead in 9. The All India United Democratic Front (AIUDF) led in 2 seats, with Raijor Dal (RJRD) and the United People’s Party, Liberal (UPPL) leading in 2 and 1 seats respectively.    Amid these developments, Prime Minister Narendra Modi is scheduled to visit the Bharatiya Janata Party headquarters in New Delhi on Monday evening as early trends show strong gains for the party in West Bengal and Assam.    &quot;Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji will visit BJP HQ, New Delhi today at 6 PM,&quot; BJP chief spokesperson Anil Baluni said in a post on X.

articles.title: Assembly election results: How many states are now ruled by BJP and allies
articles.snippet: With West Bengal likely to fall, the BJP will add another chief minister to its growing roster across the country.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: With West Bengal likely to fall, the BJP will add another chief minister to its growing roster across the country.
articles.body: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is set to expand its political footprint in India, with West Bengal emerging as the latest state set to come under its control. The party is on course for its first-ever victory in the state, leading in 197 of the 294 Assembly constituencies, according to data from the Election Commission of India at 3:40 pm.    The All India Trinamool Congress, led by Mamata Banerjee, is trailing significantly with around 90 seats.    With West Bengal likely to fall, the BJP will add another chief minister to its growing roster across the country. In Assam, the party is also set to retain power, with Himanta Biswa Sarma consolidating his position.    India currently has 28 states and 8 Union Territories, and BJP already has its own chief ministers in 16 of them. If trends hold, West Bengal will become the 17th state where the party has its own leader at the helm.    List of states where BJP has its own chief minister  • Assam: Himanta Biswa Sarma    • Arunachal Pradesh: Pema Khandu    • Bihar: Samrat Choudhary    • Chhattisgarh: Vishnu Deo Sai    • Delhi: Rekha Gupta    • Goa: Pramod Sawant    • Gujarat: Bhupendra Patel    • Haryana: Nayab Singh Saini    • Madhya Pradesh: Mohan Yadav    • Maharashtra: Devendra Fadnavis    • Manipur: Yumnam Khemchand Singh    • Odisha: Mohan Charan Majhi    • Rajasthan: Bhajan Lal Sharma    • Tripura: Manik Saha    • Uttar Pradesh: Yogi Adityanath    • Uttarakhand: Pushkar Singh Dhami    • West Bengal- To be declared    Moreover, BJP is in power in four more states and UTs through its alliance partners. However, the party does not have chief ministers of its own in these states. These are Andhra Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Sikkim and Puducherry.

articles.title: Kerala election results 2026: Full list of winners and their constituencies

The Congress-led UDF is gaining significant ground as counting gathers momentum, with initial trends indicating trouble for the ruling front. At least a dozen ministers are currently trailing in their respective constituencies.    Early figures suggest the UDF is ahead in around 100 seats, while the CPI(M)-led Left Democratic Front lags behind in second place. The BJP, which showed early promise with leads in about ten seats, has since slipped, now ahead in just two. articles.title: The invisible hand: How RSS' grassroots push powered BJP's Bengal victory
articles.snippet: Unlike traditional electioneering, the RSS strategy in Bengal relied less on large rallies and more on hyper-local engagement.
articles.author: Deblina Halder
articles.description: Unlike traditional electioneering, the RSS strategy in Bengal relied less on large rallies and more on hyper-local engagement.
articles.body: As vote counting continues in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections, the BJP’s stellar show in early trends has once again turned the spotlight on the role of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), whose quiet but extensive grassroots mobilisation is being seen as a key factor behind the party’s performance.    While the campaign was dominated by high-decibel speeches from leaders like Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, much of the groundwork in Bengal was carried out by the Sangh Parivar’s network, working through volunteers, affiliated organisations and local outreach initiatives.    While final results are still awaited, early trends suggest that the BJP’s gains in a politically complex state like West Bengal are not just the product of headline-grabbing rallies or central leadership, but of a sustained, years-long expansion of grassroots networks.    The RSS, widely regarded as the ideological parent of the BJP, has historically maintained a formal distance from electoral politics. Yet, its organisational strength, built through shakhas (local units), affiliated bodies, and a vast volunteer base, often becomes a critical force multiplier during elections.    In Bengal, where the BJP has struggled for decades to gain a foothold, this network has steadily expanded over the past decade. From a limited presence, the Sangh ecosystem now runs thousands of shakhas and outreach platforms, allowing it to penetrate rural, tribal and border regions that were once beyond its reach.  The “silent campaign”: small meetings, deep reach    Unlike traditional electioneering, the RSS strategy in Bengal relied less on large rallies and more on hyper-local engagement.    Volunteers, swayamsevaks, religious figures and affiliates, held small meetings in homes, temples, tea stalls and community spaces. The idea was simple - build trust through familiarity rather than spectacle.    A senior RSS functionary told reporters during the campaign that the focus was on “reaching every family” and maintaining continuous contact. According to ground reports, this translated into lakhs of small “voter awareness” meetings across constituencies, most of them outside the media spotlight.    Mobilising turnout: from messaging to execution    A key component of this strategy was voter mobilisation.    Campaigns built around slogans like “Pehle matdan, phir jalpan” (vote first, eat later) encouraged early turnout, particularly among core support bases. Volunteers followed up through phone calls, WhatsApp groups and local networks, ensuring that voters not only engaged with the message but also turned up on polling day.    Sources involved in the campaign said there was also a concerted effort to discourage NOTA voting and maximise participation at the booth level.    Building a broader ecosystem: beyond the BJP    The RSS effort in Bengal extended beyond its own cadre base.    Nearly three dozen religious and social organisations, along with multiple Sangh affiliates, from student groups to labour unions, were mobilised to expand outreach. In border districts, organisations like Seemanta Chetana Mancha focused on issues such as national security, while in tribal and tea garden regions, long-term social work and community engagement formed the backbone of the strategy.    RSS leaders have, however, publicly downplayed their direct electoral role.    Managing the BJP’s internal dynamics    Beyond voter outreach, the RSS also played a crucial role in organisational coordination.    In the run-up to the elections, “samanway baithaks” (coordination meetings) were held to bridge gaps within the BJP’s state unit, particularly between long-time party workers and newer entrants. This was seen as an attempt to avoid the factionalism that had affected the party’s 2021 campaign.    The Sangh’s ability to act as a neutral arbiter within the broader ideological family helped maintain cohesion during a high-stakes election.    Why Bengal was a unique challenge    For the RSS and the BJP, Bengal has never been an easy terrain.    The state’s strong regional identity, history of Left politics, and what scholars describe as a distinct strand of “Bengali Hinduism” have historically limited the appeal of the Sangh’s north Indian–centred idioms. Urban centres like Kolkata, shaped by the bhadralok tradition, have been particularly resistant.    Yet, over the past decade, shifts in political alignments, especially after the decline of the Left and the rise of Mamata Banerjee’s Trinamool Congress, have opened new spaces. The BJP’s growth has been most visible in rural belts, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe-dominated areas, and regions like north Bengal and Jungle Mahal.    The polarisation debate    The RSS’s intensified outreach has also drawn sharp political reactions.    TMC supremo Mamata Banerjee repeatedly targeted the Sangh during the campaign, framing the election as a contest between her party’s welfare-driven governance model and what she described as a “divisive mobilisation effort.”    Meanwhile, RSS-linked sources have described their campaign as one focused on “cultural awareness” and “social awakening,” rather than direct political messaging.    In addition, alongside the RSS’ grassroots push, much of the BJP’s electoral architecture in Bengal reflects the strategic imprint of Home Minister Shah, often described as the party’s chief election strategist. Shah’s emphasis on booth-level management, data-driven targeting and tight organisational control has shaped how the BJP converts social outreach into votes.    The RSS network, in this framework, functioned as a force multiplier, feeding local intelligence, sustaining voter contact and ensuring turnout.    As counting continues, the 2026 Bengal election is being viewed as a test of whether this long-term organisational groundwork can translate into durable electoral gains.    If current trends hold, the RSS’s “invisible hand” may well prove to be one of the defining factors behind the BJP’s push in one of India’s most politically challenging states.

articles.title: TVK's VS Babu defeats sitting Tamil Nadu CM MK Stalin from Kolathur seat
articles.snippet: Babu arrived at Loyola College counting centre to collect his winning certificate, reported ANI.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Babu arrived at Loyola College counting centre to collect his winning certificate, reported ANI.
articles.body: The incumbent Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and President of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam suffered defeat to TVK’s candidate Babu from the Kolathur seat. Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)'s candidate Babu is leading by a margin of 8795 after the completion of all 22 rounds of counting, according to the Election Commission of India (ECI).    Babu arrived at Loyola College counting centre and collected his winning certificate, reported ANI.    #WAYCJ | TVK candidate from Kolathur constituency, VS Babu, collects his winning certificate at the Loyola College counting centre, defeating Tamil Nadu CM MK Stalin. pic.twitter.com/ddrf0ajF2j  — ANI (@ANI) May 4, 2026      Stalin was among 14 DMK ministers who were trailing in their respective constituencies even after the third round of counting.    Meanwhile, in a dramatic electoral development in the Tamil Nadu Assembly elections 2026, TVK chief and actor Vijay's family was seen celebrating at their residence as the party continued its strong lead across the state, with early projections placing it ahead in 110 of the total 234 seats.    The celebrations at Vijay's home were marked by joy and music, with family members dancing and singing the song 'Whistle Podu' from his film 'The Greatest of All Time.'    The track also holds significance as it is associated with the party's identity. Vijay's family members, including cousins, were present during the celebrations as the trends updates showed the party maintaining its lead.    According to the latest counting trends, TVK has emerged as the single-largest party in the state, with a broader political impact already visible across constituencies.    Projections indicated the party leading in 110 constituencies. That leaaves TVK 8 short of the halfway mark a number that is likely to be made up of smaller parties that were part of either the DMK or the AIADMK alliance.    The political landscape in Tamil Nadu witnessed a major shift as counting of votes began at 8 am on Monday, with results still awaiting official declaration by the Election Commission.    AIADMK was ahead in 64 constituencies, while DMK was leading in 44 seats. Smaller parties, including Pattali Makkal Katchi (PMK), Indian National Congress (INC), and Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), were leading in 4, 5, and 3 seats, respectively.

articles.title: 'If BJP wins Bengal, SP will struggle to even reach 40 seats in Uttar Pradesh. You can write that down'
articles.snippet: For the Samajwadi Party, the Bengal trends pose a more immediate challenge. Akhilesh Yadav has consistently positioned Mamata Banerjee as a key face of resistance against the BJP. If that resistance appears to weaken, it risks affecting the opposition’s broader narrative that the BJP can be defeated through united efforts.
articles.author: Biswajeet Banerjee
articles.description: For the Samajwadi Party, the Bengal trends pose a more immediate challenge. Akhilesh Yadav has consistently positioned Mamata Banerjee as a key face of resistance against the BJP. If that resistance appears to weaken, it risks affecting the opposition’s broader narrative that the BJP can be defeated through united efforts.
articles.body: As counting trends in West Bengal show the BJP in the lead, the political message is already travelling beyond Kolkata to the Hindi heartland. The early numbers have triggered sharp reactions across parties, with one Congress MP telling this reporter, “If these trends hold and BJP takes Bengal, the opposition’s game in Uttar Pradesh becomes very difficult. You can note it down, SP will struggle to even touch 40 seats.”    The remark captures the larger political undercurrent. Even before the final results, the perception battle has begun. In Indian politics, momentum often matters as much as arithmetic, and a BJP lead in Bengal is fast being read as a signal of expanding dominance.    A key factor in the BJP’s surge in West Bengal has been the aggressive campaign led by Yogi Adityanath, who emerged as one of the party’s most visible faces on the ground. His rallies injected a sharper ideological pitch into the contest, blending themes of law and order, welfare delivery and cultural identity.    By repeatedly invoking what he described as the “Uttar Pradesh model,” Adityanath sought to present a contrast between governance under the BJP and the existing regime in Bengal. His speeches, marked by strong messaging on security and development, helped consolidate core supporters while energising cadre at the grassroots. Party leaders believe his campaign played a crucial role in polarising the narrative and expanding the BJP’s appeal beyond its traditional base, turning the Bengal election into a more direct ideological contest.    For the BJP, leading in a state long considered a stronghold of Mamata Banerjee is not just an electoral development but a narrative shift. The party is likely to project this as proof that its political and ideological appeal is no longer regionally limited. From Kolkata, the message being crafted is one of national acceptability and organisational depth.    In Uttar Pradesh, this could translate into renewed confidence within the BJP cadre. After a less than expected performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in the state, a strong showing in Bengal offers psychological recovery. Party workers are likely to interpret this as validation that even the toughest political fortresses can be breached.    Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s governance model is expected to be central to this messaging. The BJP may argue that the same template of welfare delivery, infrastructure push and law and order has found resonance beyond Uttar Pradesh. This could help consolidate urban voters and sections of the middle class who prioritise stability and development.    At the ground level, such momentum often strengthens booth level mobilisation. A perception that the party is on a winning trajectory can energise workers, improve turnout management and attract fence sitting voters. Political observers describe this as the bandwagon effect, where voters align with the side they see as ascendant.    However, this advantage is not without risks. A strong external victory can sometimes lead to overconfidence. In Uttar Pradesh, local issues such as unemployment, price rise, agrarian distress and stray cattle remain critical. If these concerns are overshadowed by a national narrative, it could create disconnect, particularly in rural areas.    For the Samajwadi Party, the Bengal trends pose a more immediate challenge. Akhilesh Yadav has consistently positioned Mamata Banerjee as a key face of resistance against the BJP. If that resistance appears to weaken, it risks affecting the opposition’s broader narrative that the BJP can be defeated through united efforts.    The impact is likely to be both psychological and strategic. Within the SP cadre, there could be concerns about momentum and morale. Among voters, especially minorities and younger sections looking for change, the perception of a dominant BJP could create hesitation.    Alliance dynamics may also shift. Smaller regional players often calibrate their positions based on perceived winners. A BJP surge in Bengal could make alignment with the ruling party seem a safer political choice, potentially complicating the SP’s coalition building efforts ahead of 2027.    At the same time, the SP is not without its counter strategy. The party has been working to expand its social base, reaching out to non Yadav OBC groups while consolidating its core support. It has sharpened its campaign around livelihood issues, attempting to localise the electoral discourse in Uttar Pradesh.    Yet, what makes the Bengal trends particularly significant is the speed at which political messaging travels. There is a strong socioeconomic linkage between Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, with migrant workers and community networks acting as informal carriers of political sentiment. What unfolds in Kolkata often finds its way into conversations in towns and villages across Uttar Pradesh.    If the BJP converts its lead into a decisive victory, it will likely frame the result as a mandate for its governance and ideological plank, reinforcing its pitch ahead of 2027. If the trends reverse, the opposition will be quick to reclaim the narrative.    For now, as counting continues, one thing is clear. The battle for Uttar Pradesh in 2027 is already being shaped, and the first signals are coming from Bengal. The road from Kolkata to Lucknow has become politically shorter than ever.

articles.title: From hero to rival: How Vijay turned the tables on his first producer Udhayanidhi Stalin
articles.snippet: Until now, his political story has been about proving he can uphold and extend a family legacy. This election result pushes him into a sharper contest, where lineage alone offers less protection.
articles.author: Manisha Lal Khandpur
articles.description: Until now, his political story has been about proving he can uphold and extend a family legacy. This election result pushes him into a sharper contest, where lineage alone offers less protection.
articles.body: A film producer backing a rising star in 2008 could hardly have imagined this script twist. Ruling DMK's Udhayanidhi Stalin’s first production venture, Kuruvi, had actor Vijay in the lead. Today the same Vijay has emerged as a key disruptor for Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) through his party Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK).  What began as a shared phase in cinema has turned into a direct political face-off.    A political heir with a familiar path    Udhayanidhi Stalin’s entry in the DMK was naturally seen as the party's extension of the legacy. Grandson of M Karunanidhi and son of MK Stalin his entry into political arena was bound to happen.    Even his climbing the ladder within the party was largely structured. He started as a leader in the youth wing, got visibility on campaign stage and marked his first electoral victory, a cabinet post and then the deputy chief minister’s chair.    What set him apart was not just his surname, but when and how he arrived.    Cinema, visibility and a new DMK face    Even as Udhayanidhi entered frontline politics, despite his popular last name, he missed some things like mass aura of MGR or the ideological weight of Karunanidhi, but he had something suited to a new era- visibility.    His decades long career in the film industry first as a producer and then as an actor fetched him visibility more than popularity. The DMK used that familiarity to reach younger voters who were not consuming politics in a traditional way, but rather through social media.    His role was more calibrated: to update the party’s communication, front its generational shift and link a legacy-driven organisation to a media-savvy electorate.    For a period, that strategy seemed to work.    From 2019 to 2021: Validation for the experiment    Udhayanidhi appeared to justify the DMK’s investment in him during 2019 Lok Sabha polls and the 2021 Assembly. He helped party expand its reach by using ponline campaigns among other things.    His win from Chepauk-Thiruvallikeni was emphatic, quietening doubts about his electoral strength. Inside the DMK, his rise began to look less like a forced promotion and more like a natural progression.    That is what makes the current setback significant.    A new kind of opponent    A defeat at the hands of Vijay’s TVK does not immediately alter Udhayanidhi Stalin’s position within the DMK. The succession plan remains. He is still seen as the future leader, still central to the party’s long-term strategy. Tamil Nadu’s political culture rarely overturns internal hierarchies after a single electoral shock.    But this result introduces a new element into his political journey.    It brings in a rival his father did not quite face.    MK Stalin’s principal adversary for much of his rise was the AIADMK, led by figures like Jayalalithaa, who, despite their own film backgrounds, operated firmly within established party structures and the familiar contours of Dravidian politics.    Vijay alters that landscape.    From star power to political capital    Vijay carries a different kind of authority into politics. His strength does not come from organisational depth or ideological inheritance, but from his status as a long-standing box-office draw with a devoted fan base.    That kind of cultural capital can be converted quickly into votes.    Udhayanidhi’s own film career, while politically useful, was never intended to create that scale of fandom. The DMK did not need him to be a larger-than-life figure; it needed him to be efficient and relatable. Vijay, in contrast, enters politics with a ready-made emotional following that does not require years of party-building.    That imbalance is now exposed.    From inheritance to contest    So the nature of Udhayanidhi’s challenge changes.    Until now, his political story has been about proving he can uphold and extend a family legacy. This election result pushes him into a sharper contest, where lineage alone offers less protection.    He must now define himself not only in relation to the expectations of his party, but also in comparison with a rival who operates outside the traditional Dravidian framework, drawing strength from the world of cinema that first brought them together.    The doors in the DMK remain open for Udhayanidhi Stalin. But the arena he steps into has changed and so have the rules of engagement between cinema and politics in Tamil Nadu.

articles.title: Vijay is breakout star as TN stares at hung assembly: Who will be the new CM?
articles.snippet: Data by the Election Commission shows Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) emerging as the single-largest party with around 110 seats
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Data by the Election Commission shows Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) emerging as the single-largest party with around 110 seats
articles.body: Tamil Nadu is heading towards a hung assembly, with no party or alliance crossing the majority mark of 118 in the 234-member House, according to the latest trends on May 4.    Data by the Election Commission shows Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) emerging as the single-largest party with around 106 seats, followed by the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) at 56 seats and All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) at 53 seats.    The fractured verdict is largely attributed to TVK’s entry, which split votes in a three-way contest involving DMK and AIADMK, along with high voter turnout.    With no clear majority, post-poll alliances are likely to decide government formation, making the final outcome uncertain.    What happens next?    If the state doesn’t get a clear mandate after counting concludes, post-poll negotiations are expected to be crucial. TVK, as the likely single largest party, may explore support from other groups or factions and may also get support from smaller parties of both Dravidian alliances.    While TVK is currently ahead, it remains uncertain whether it will cross the 118-seat majority mark on its own or fall short, potentially resulting in a hung assembly and positioning Vijay as the key player in government formation.    Counting is still underway across the 234 assembly seats, and a clear picture of the verdict would be out only by evening.    Who will be the likely chief minister of Tamil Nadu?    If TVK forms the government in Tamil Nadu 2026, actor-turned-politician C Joseph Vijay is widely expected to be the chief minister.    TVK has projected Vijay as its CM face from the start. He is also contesting from Perambur and Tiruchirappalli East, where he is currently leading as per trends.    With the party ahead but still uncertain to cross the 118-seat majority mark, the possibility of a hung assembly remains open.    In such a scenario, any post-poll arrangement -- whether TVK forms a government alone or with support -- would likely revolve around Vijay as CM. The party has consistently maintained that leadership will not be negotiable, making him the central figure in Tamil Nadu’s next government formation.    &quot;Our leader Thalapathy Vijay will rule Tamil Nadu tomorrow with a visionary mind. The 2026 election victory will be historic,&quot; said TVK executive committee chief coordinator KA Sengottaiyan ahead of the verdict.    Vijay's father and former director, SA Chandrasekhar, on Monday looked back at his son's journey to become the chief minister hopeful today.    &quot;I am motivated. As a human, you should not only be an artist, you should have some social thinking. For the last 30 years, he (Vijay) had something in his mind, that he has to do something for Tamil Nadu. Today he is going to be chief minister,&quot; he told ANI as trends showed TVK ahead in Tamil Nadu race.

articles.title: Vijay's 'vijay' throws Stalin off script: Road ahead for DMK
articles.snippet: Early trends indicate a significant setback for the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) led by M. K. Stalin, which had entered the contest with expectations of retaining power and strong projections in most exit polls.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Early trends indicate a significant setback for the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) led by M. K. Stalin, which had entered the contest with expectations of retaining power and strong projections in most exit polls.
articles.body: Visuals from the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) headquarters suggest cadres gradually packing up for the day, as counting continues across Tamil Nadu and the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) edges closer to the majority mark of 118 seats required to form government in the 234-member Assembly.    CM MK Stalin faces tough contest in Kolathur    M. K. Stalin is reported to be facing a tough fight in Kolathur against TVK’s VK Babu, who is leading by more than 8000 votes in early trends. M. K. Stalin, contesting from Kolathur, has held the seat since 2011 and secured successive wins, including a decisive 2021 victory by a margin of 70,384 votes. However, early trends suggest he is trailing in the constituency.    TVK, AIADMK and DMK seat trends    TVK is leading on 110 seats, the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (ADMK) on 58, and DMK on 49 seats.    Govt officials, ministers responsible for defeat, says Stalin's kin Jaya Rajamurthy, DMK Chief MK Stalin’s brother-in-law, said in a post on Facebook that “some government officials and ministers are responsible for the party’s defeat”.    According to the latest trends, TVK is leading in 108 seats, the AIADMK-led coalition in 69 seats, and the DMK-led alliance in 57 seats.    Can DMK form an alliance?    DMK is most unlikely to form an alliance with the emerging party TVK, even as reports recall earlier political outreach suggestions, including TVK alliance discussions linked to Congress by Vijay's father. Vijay’s father, SA Chandrasekhar, has previously invited the Congress to consider an alliance with Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), stating the actor-turned-politician is willing to share power and has a strong emotional connect with voters across age groups.    What's next for DMK?     The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) is likely to emerge as the principal opposition party if early trends persist and no major shifts are seen in the final rounds of counting.    What led to DMK loss - The Vijay Factor?    Emergence of TVK (2026): TVK is reportedly drawing away a portion of the DMK alliance’s vote base, with growing sentiment among voters seeking change from established Dravidian parties.    Based on May 2026 election trends, the DMK is facing a strong anti-incumbency wave in Tamil Nadu, with several ministers trailing in early rounds. Voter dissatisfaction linked to governance issues, tax concerns, and local grievances appears to have benefited alternatives like TVK and AIADMK.    The ruling DMK’s setback marks a significant shift in Tamil Nadu’s political landscape. Once a dominant force alongside AIADMK, the party’s position slipping to third in early trends is being viewed as one of the biggest developments of the election.    For decades, Tamil Nadu politics has been defined by the DMK–AIADMK rivalry, but current trends suggest that the traditional binary may be breaking down amid the rising influence of the “Vijay factor.”

articles.title: 10 takeaways from 2026 election results: BJP's Bengal bloom, Vijay's TN blockbuster, Cong's Kerala...
articles.snippet: BJP is set to make history in West Bengal after edging out TMC in a largely one-sided contest while superstar Vijay has emerged as the dominant political force in Tamil Nadu in his first ever election.
articles.author: Armaan Bhatnagar
articles.description: BJP is set to make history in West Bengal after edging out TMC in a largely one-sided contest while superstar Vijay has emerged as the dominant political force in Tamil Nadu in his first ever election.
articles.body: The 2026 assembly election was a story of two remarkable performances and a spirited comeback with the BJP-led NDA securing a 3-5 scoreline in this year's only electoral cycle.    BJP on Monday clinched the crown jewel of the country's eastern flank after unseating the formidable Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress in West Bengal. The party is now set to form its first-ever government in the state which has only been ruled by either TMC or the Left for nearly 50 years.    In Tamil Nadu, actor-turned-politician Vijay's TVK emerged as a powerful disruptor with a blockbuster debut that upended the bipolar Dravidian dominance of both DMK and AIADMK - the two alliances that have been the mainstay of the state's politics for six decades.    Kerala saw winds of change with the state reposing faith in the Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) after giving back-to-back terms to its rival Left Democratic Front (LDF). In Assam and Puducherry, NDA secured comfortable victories and cemented its footprint in key northeast and southern bastions.    Here are the big takeaways from assembly elections 2026:    Sunrise on BJP’s eastern flank: In a state that traditionally leans Left, BJP had its task cut out when it set out on a mission to expand its footprint in Bengal. The party won just three seats in the 2016 elections and was barely a marginal player in the state. Within a decade, BJP has charted one of the most striking growth arcs in Indian history, carving a significant space for itself in the ideologically-driven landscape of West Bengal. Trends show that BJP is ahead in over 195 of the state's 294 seats, while TMC lags with leads in just 95. On the verge of forming its first-ever government in the state, BJP has completed a fulfilling political journey in the state and dealt a crushing blow to one of opposition's most powerful leaders in Mamata Banerjee.    'Sun' sets on DMK, 'star' rises in TN: Indian elections are not usually kind to debutants given the sheer political machinery and institutional strength required to woo crores of voters. However, the immense star power of Vijay and the growing voter fatigue with the two Dravidian giants—DMK and AIADMK—gave Tamil Nadu one of the most surprising results in recent history. On debut, Vijay's TVK is leading in over 108 of the state's 234 seats, emerging as the single largest party and seizing the strongest claim to the chief minister's chair. Vijay's blockbuster debut brushed aside both the fronts led by DMK and AIADMK, who are leading in 63 seats each. While it remains to be seen how post-poll alliances play out in Tamil Nadu, it is clear that Vijay is the true superstar of this election. It is also clear that voters are now ready to break out of the familar mould of Tamil Nadu politics, seeking a real change in 2026.    Modi magic wipes out opposition: The BJP continues to dominate the length and breadth of India's political landscape without showing signs of fatigue with Prime Minister Narendra Modi leading the charge from the front. In West Bengal, PM Modi addressed over a dozen rallies and fronted the party's campaign, focusing on wooing the women voters, targeting TMC over infiltration and using his characteristic tone to mock Didi (Mamata). Modi's national appeal and his guarantees for Bengal struck a chord with the voters yet again, helping BJP complete its dominance in the east after conquering Odisha in 2024 and installing its own CM in Bihar last month.    Mamata finds no 'Mamata' in Bengal: Eyeing a historic fourth term, Mamata's formidable fortress finally fell to BJP's dominant electoral machinery with the TMC failing to convert the chief minister's fighting spirit into seats. A crumbling state of law and order, incidents like RG Kar and Sandeshkhali, voter disillusionment and growing anger over TMC 'tolabaazi' prompted voters to choose &quot;poriborton&quot; (change) over continuity. Initial data suggests that even Mamata's traditional voters, the women, ditched TMC in the election with the BJP ahead in 35 out of the 39 seats where women voters outnumber their male counterparts.    Kerala returns to a familiar pattern: Chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan scripted history five years ago after retaining the mandate of the people in a state which is known to vote out the incumbent. Most observers credited the victory to the Covid-era measures by the government that led to voter consolidation in favour of the ruling LDF in 2021. However, dogged by anti-incumbency, corruption charges and charges of changing characteristic of the Left itself, CPM found it too hard to extend its tenure by five more years. On the other hand, Kerala is now back in UDF's hands. The Congress-led alliance is ahead in 100 of the 140 seats of the state in a result that will give the grand old party a boost in spirit as it seeks to protect its significance in the south, a region where BJP is yet to dominate.    Himanta hattrick in Assam: The BJP-led NDA is leading in nearly 100 of the state's 126 seats and is set to deliver its most dominant performance in Assam, completely brushing aside even the remotest talk of anti-incumbency. BJP's bet on chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has clearly reaped rich dividends in the state as the party strongman delivered Assam for the party for the third time after a highly polarised campaign.    Trouble for INDIA bloc: The election results spell further trouble for the opposition INDIA bloc which saw a brief, yet encouraging, revival after the 2024 Lok Sabha polls. With NDA proving that 2024 general election was just an abberation, the opposition is now again facing an existential crisis as the BJP looks determined to reduce all rival parties to the margins. Moreover, with the sidelining of Mamata Banerjee and MK Stalin, two of the most vocal BJP opponents in the national space, the opposition will find itself on the backfoot on the road to 2029 Lok Sabha polls.    Congress now first among equals: While Congress failed to pose any challenge in Assam or make any meaningful gains in Tamil Nadu, the party silently secured its credentials as the primary challenger to the BJP with both Mamata and Stalin facing defeats in the election. For long, Congress had been facing calls to step aside and let leaders like Mamata take the centrestage within the INDIA bloc after failing to take the fight to BJP. While the grand old party has not made much gains across India, its position as the de facto leader of the INDIA bloc remains protected, for now.    Road to UP and beyond: The election results leave BJP with a strong momentum ahead of the Uttar Pradesh polls, coming on the back of victories in Haryana, Maharashtra, Bihar and Delhi. RSS also played a crucial role for BJP in Bengal, helping the party boost its grassroots presence and consolidate Hindu voters. RSS activated its shakhas and affiliates to penetrate Hindu communities, framing the election as a &quot;battle for Hindu existence&quot; against TMC's alleged appeasement politics. RSS' role will be even more pronounced in Uttar Pradesh with Sangh already activing its cadre a year before the polling. With Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur and Goa also heading to the polls next year, the BJP enters the next electoral cycle with a clear advantage over the opposition and formidable cadre strength.    Exit polls were a hit &amp;amp; miss: As always, exit poll predictions did not exactly hit the bull's eye but some turned out to be quite accurate. Most pollsters, including VoteVibe broadcast by CNN-News18, had predicted a BJP victory in the state. Axis My India predicted a TVK sweep in the Tamil Nadu election along with one other pollster, which also proved to be correct though a majority had forecast a DMK victory. Most pollsters also predicted a UDF comeback in Kerala and an easy Assam win for BJP. While predictions around seat count varied, the overall outcome turned out to be correct.

articles.title: From jhalmuri stop to seat sweep: How PM Modi’s viral moment played out in West Bengal's Jhargram
articles.snippet: West Bengal Election Results 2026: A brief roadside jhalmuri stop by PM Modi in Jhargram turned into a viral moment, later becoming part of the political narrative in Bengal.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: West Bengal Election Results 2026: A brief roadside jhalmuri stop by PM Modi in Jhargram turned into a viral moment, later becoming part of the political narrative in Bengal.
articles.body: A roadside snack in Jhargram has unexpectedly turned into a talking point in the West Bengal Assembly elections. What began as a brief pause during a campaign trail has now become part of a larger political narrative, as early trends show the Bharatiya Janata Party gaining ground in the very region where Prime Minister Narendra Modi stopped to eat jhalmuri.    The BJP is currently leading across all four seats in Jhargram district, including Nayagram, Gopiballavpur, Jhargram, and Binpur. This region, part of the Junglemahal belt, has long been seen as economically underdeveloped, with Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes making up nearly half the population. Their voting patterns often play a decisive role, and this time, the trend appears to favour the BJP.    The viral moment that sparked debate    During his campaign in April, PM Modi made an unscheduled stop at a small roadside stall in Jhargram. Asking the vendor, “Bhai, humein apna jhalmuri khilao,” he ordered a simple ₹10 portion of the snack and insisted on paying for it himself.    The interaction quickly went viral, not just for its spontaneity but also for the Prime Minister’s humour. When asked about onions, he responded, “Haan, pyaaz khata hoon, dimaag nahi.”    For supporters, the moment reflected a relatable side of the Prime Minister, someone willing to pause his schedule to engage with everyday life. For critics, particularly the Trinamool Congress, it was dismissed as a carefully staged photo opportunity. The party even pointed out that the stall itself had been built under the state government’s initiative.    More than just a snack    Jhalmuri is not just a popular street food in Bengal. It carries a certain cultural familiarity, a connection to everyday life across the state. Modi’s decision to stop and eat it was widely seen as an attempt to bridge the outsider versus insider narrative that has often dominated Bengal politics.    The BJP has long faced the “bahiragoto” label from the TMC. By embracing a local symbol, the party appeared to be making a subtle political statement, positioning itself as more in tune with Bengal’s cultural identity.    That symbolism seems to have found some resonance on the ground, at least in Jhargram.    What the numbers suggest    Jhargram is one of the 294 assembly constituencies in the state and is classified as semi-urban. This time, the contest has largely been a direct fight between the BJP and the TMC, with candidates like Laxmikant Sahu for the BJP and Mongal Saren for the TMC.    Initial trends indicate that the BJP has taken the lead in the constituency, mirroring its broader performance in the district. If these trends hold, it would mark a significant breakthrough for the party in a region where electoral outcomes often hinge on local issues and identity politics.    The larger takeaway    The so-called “jhalmuri moment” may appear trivial at first glance, but it fits into a broader campaign strategy. Political messaging today is not limited to speeches and rallies. Small, symbolic gestures can carry weight, especially when they resonate with local culture.    In Jhargram, that message seems to have connected. Whether it was the snack, the symbolism, or a combination of factors, the BJP’s performance here points to a shift that goes beyond a single campaign stop.    As the results continue to unfold, one thing is evident. Sometimes, even the smallest moments can leave a lasting political impact.

articles.title: Mamata and Stalin: Why INDIA bloc’s biggest faces were 2026 elections' biggest flops
articles.snippet: BJP is poised to unseat Mamata in Bengal, while Vijay’s election debut will see Stalin's ouster in Tamil Nadu
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: BJP is poised to unseat Mamata in Bengal, while Vijay’s election debut will see Stalin's ouster in Tamil Nadu
articles.body: India’s Opposition alliance suffered a major blow on May 4, with two of its most powerful regional leaders facing potential electoral setbacks ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha polls.    The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is poised to end Mamata Banerjee’s bid for a fourth term in West Bengal, leading in a commanding number of seats in the 294-member Assembly. In Tamil Nadu, MK Stalin is also facing a serious challenge, with actor-turned-politician Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) emerging as a major disruptor.    Stalin and Banerjee are among the most prominent faces of the INDIA bloc, collectively commanding significant influence in the Lok Sabha. Both leaders have been key figures in resisting the BJP’s expansion in their respective states, with Banerjee often seen as a potential national challenger to Narendra Modi.    With the Indian National Congress struggling in recent state elections, questions had already emerged over Rahul Gandhi’s positioning as the Opposition’s central face. A setback for both Banerjee and Stalin could further reshape leadership dynamics within the bloc and potentially open space for the BJP ahead of 2029.    What may have gone wrong    Mamata’s challenge    Banerjee came to power in 2011, ending the Communist Party of India (Marxist)’s three-decade rule, and consolidated her position in 2016 and 2021 despite a rising BJP challenge.    However, after over a decade in power, anti-incumbency appears to have set in. Concerns around law and order, crimes against women—including the RG Kar case—along with allegations of corruption and limited job creation may have contributed to voter discontent.    Stalin under pressure    The DMK returned to power in 2021 after defeating the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK), winning 133 of 234 seats. But this election signals a potential shift in Tamil Nadu’s political landscape.    Since 1967, when CN Annadurai led the DMK to power, the state has largely been dominated by the DMK and AIADMK. The emergence of TVK suggests possible voter fatigue with this long-standing duopoly.    Frequent confrontations between the DMK government and the Centre—over issues such as education policy, language, and fiscal federalism—may also have influenced sections of voters who prioritise governance and economic outcomes.    The ‘Vijay factor’    Analysts attribute a significant part of TVK’s surge to Vijay’s personal appeal, especially among youth and women voters. Popularly known as “Thalapathy”, he entered politics with a massive fan base built over a three-decade film career since his debut in Vetri (1984). His crossover from cinema to politics appears to have translated into electoral traction.    BJP’s expanding footprint    The BJP’s performance reflects its continued organisational push beyond its traditional strongholds. A strong showing in West Bengal—after falling short in previous attempts—marks a significant milestone.    Following the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, the party has strengthened its position in multiple states, including Maharashtra, Haryana, Bihar, Delhi and Odisha. Gains in West Bengal could further widen the NDA’s geographic reach.    Alongside electoral machinery, factors such as grassroots mobilisation, organisational support from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, and targeted welfare outreach are seen as contributing to its rise. The Special Intensive Revision, which removed several lakh voters from the roll, may have also contributed to the victory.    Opposition unity under strain    The Opposition’s inability to maintain a united front in the 2026 state elections may also have played a role. Unlike the 2024 Lok Sabha polls, several INDIA bloc partners contested independently, potentially splitting anti-BJP votes.    In Tamil Nadu, friction between the DMK and Congress over seat-sharing, along with internal differences on alliances, highlighted coordination challenges within the bloc.    The 2026 results, if trends hold, could mark a turning point—weakening two of the Opposition’s strongest regional pillars while giving the BJP fresh momentum ahead of the next national election cycle.

articles.title: No 'Left' left? For 1st time since 1970s, India to have no Communist CM as last bastion crumbles
articles.snippet: The Pinarayi Vijayan-led Left Democratic Front government in Kerala, which came to power in 2016, was the last Communist outpost that crumbled today.
articles.author: Chhabi Kala
articles.description: The Pinarayi Vijayan-led Left Democratic Front government in Kerala, which came to power in 2016, was the last Communist outpost that crumbled today.
articles.body: With the CPI(M)-led Left government headed for a crushing defeat in Kerala, the red that once dominated India’s political map now survives only in fragments.    Left parties such as the Communist Party of India (CPI), Communist Party of India (Marxist) or CPI(M), and Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) Liberation or CPI(ML) Liberation continue to retain organisational presence, but their national footprint has steadily declined.    From peak power to shrinking footprint    In the 1980s, Left parties — led by the CPI(M) — held their strongest position, governing Kerala, Tripura and West Bengal simultaneously. In the Lok Sabha, their peak came in 2004, when they won over 60 seats.    The Manmohan Singh-led UPA government was forced to face a floor test after the Left Front, with nearly 60 MPs in the Lok Sabha, withdrew support over the Indo-US nuclear deal.    The Left bloc was in power in West Bengal from 1977 to 2011. It ruled Tripura from 1993 to 2018. And in Kerala, it returned to power every five years and convincingly broke the trend in 2021.    West Bengal: The Longest Rule    In 1977, the CPI(M) came to power in West Bengal, beginning the longest uninterrupted rule by any party in an Indian state. Jyoti Basu served as chief minister for over 23 years before handing over to Buddhadeb Bhattacharya in 2000. The Left would rule Bengal for 11 more years after that.    Tripura Rule    The Left ruled Tripura from 1993 to 2018. In 1993, the Left swept to power in the state, with the CPI(M) alone winning 44 of the 60 seats in the Assembly. Dasarath Deb was the chief minister till 1998, when Manik Sarkar took over and held on to the chair for 20 years.    The 25-year-old Left Front rule in Tripura came to an end with the BJP surprisingly decimating it in 2018. The BJP repeated the feat in 2023.    The Kerala Story    The Left's last bastion has crumbled with the poor showing of CPI(M) in Kerala this election cycle. According to the current counting trends, Congress-led UDF has gained a comfortable lead in the southern state.    The Pinarayi Vijayan's CPI(M)-led Left Democratic Front (LDF) government in Kerala, which came to power in 2016, was the last Communist outpost that crumbled today. For the first time since 1977, India will have no Communist chief minister.    Early Rise in Independent India    The Left's political history in India is a storied one. When the first elections were held in the country in 1951-52, it was the Communist Party of India that had the highest number of seats among Opposition parties in the Lok Sabha.    Just five years later, in 1957, India's Left parties made history by winning the elections in Kerala and forming the world's first democratically elected Communist government in any major nation.    The Left alternated power in Kerala, but another state where it enjoyed uninterrupted success for a sustained period was Tripura, that fell to BJP in 2018.

articles.title: How Vijay emerged Tamil Nadu's Jana Nayagan: Factors behind TVK's blockbuster debut
articles.snippet: This election appears to mark a shift, with TVK emerging as a serious contender in its debut
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: This election appears to mark a shift, with TVK emerging as a serious contender in its debut
articles.body: Actor-turned-politician Vijay is set for a dramatic political debut, with his party Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) closing in on the majority mark in the Tamil Nadu Assembly elections—potentially disrupting the decades-long dominance of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK).    At 2:15 pm, TVK was leading in 107 seats, while the AIADMK was ahead in 66, CNN News18 reported. Outgoing chief minister MK Stalin’s DMK trailed in third place with 61 seats.    According to the Election Commission of India website, TVK was leading in 110 constituencies, followed by AIADMK in 57 and DMK in 49. The Indian National Congress was ahead in four seats.    Here are the factors that may have fuelled Vijay’s surge    Anti-incumbency    The DMK returned to power in 2021 after ending the AIADMK’s decade-long rule. The election—held after the deaths of J Jayalalithaa and M Karunanidhi—saw the Stalin-led party win 133 of the 234 seats.    Tamil Nadu had a pattern of frequently alternating governments until 2016, when Jayalalithaa secured a consecutive term. If the DMK fails to retain power, it could signal a return to that “revolving door” trend, with anti-incumbency playing a decisive role.    Voter fatigue with Dravidian politics    This election appears to mark a shift, with TVK emerging as a serious contender in its debut. Since 1967, when CN Annadurai led the DMK to power, Tamil Nadu has been dominated by the DMK and AIADMK. The rise of TVK suggests a potential break from this long-standing duopoly.    Local issues taking centre stage    The long-running Hindi vs Tamil debate—often central to Dravidian politics—may have led to voter fatigue. Issues such as infrastructure, roads and corruption appear to have gained prominence during this election.    The DMK government’s frequent confrontations with the Centre over education, language policy, tax devolution and representation may also have contributed to voter discontent, with some perceiving it as a distraction from governance priorities.    The ‘Vijay factor’    Analysts point to Vijay’s mass appeal—especially among youth and women voters—as a key driver of TVK’s performance. Popularly known as “Thalapathy”, he entered politics with a massive fan base built over a three-decade film career since his debut as a child actor in Vetri (1984).    What exit polls had predicted    Most exit polls had projected a comfortable win for the DMK-led Secular Progressive Alliance. Agencies such as People Pulse, Matrize and P-MARQ estimated 120–145 seats for the alliance, with the AIADMK-led NDA trailing at 60–100 seats.    Interestingly, Axis My India had forecast 98–120 seats for TVK, closer to the current trends.    Tamil Nadu recorded a strong voter turnout of 82.24 percent, reflecting high participation across both urban and rural constituencies.

articles.title: Not just Kerala victory: What's the other significant takeaway for Congress in 2026 election results
articles.snippet: Kerala continues to resist the BJP’s expansion, making it one of the rare arenas where the opposition can secure a clear, direct mandate.
articles.author: Arishaa Izaj
articles.description: Kerala continues to resist the BJP’s expansion, making it one of the rare arenas where the opposition can secure a clear, direct mandate.
articles.body: The 2026 assembly election results are beginning to reshape the internal hierarchy of the INDIA bloc, with the Congress emerging in a stronger position even as key regional players stumble.    Over the past year, leaders such as Mamata Banerjee and MK Stalin were considered key figures for the opposition alliance, especially as concerns about Rahul Gandhi's role as the national leader grew amidst internal disagreements, with regional leaders providing strength against the BJP.    However, electoral defeats in West Bengal and Tamil Nadu have diminished this momentum, creating an opportunity for the Congress to restore its influence within the coalition.    In West Bengal, the scale of the shift is particularly striking. The BJP is leading in around 170 seats, potentially ending over a decade of Trinamool Congress rule. The TMC is trailing with leads in roughly 90 seats, while the Congress has struggled to make an impact, with leaders like Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury trailing in Baharampur.    The result not only weakens Mamata Banerjee’s national standing but also removes one of the strongest regional pillars of the INDIA bloc.    In Tamil Nadu, the actor-turned-politician Vijay's TVK is witnessing a remarkable surge in Tamil Nadu in his debut election, with early trends showing his party leading in over 90 out of the state's 234 seats.    Against this backdrop, Kerala has delivered a contrasting story. With the Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) ahead in 97 of Kerala’s 140 seats, the party is poised to form a government in a state where the BJP remains a marginal electoral force despite incremental gains in vote share over the years.    Kerala continues to resist the BJP’s expansion, making it one of the rare arenas where the opposition can secure a clear, direct mandate.    The scale of the UDF’s performance is notable in the historical context. Its best showing came in 2001 with 99 seats. Since then, the alliance has seen sharp fluctuations. It won 72 seats in 2011, just above the majority mark of 71, before slipping to 47 in 2016. In 2021, the Pinarayi Vijayan-led Left Democratic Front (LDF) retained power with 99 seats, reducing the UDF to 41 and breaking the state’s long-standing pattern of alternating governments. The current tally marks a significant recovery for the Congress-led alliance.    The nature of this mandate also reflects a deeper political shift. The Left’s resilience in Kerala has historically been built on its welfare architecture. Subsidies, pensions and targeted schemes ensured a steady support base, particularly among economically vulnerable groups.    But that model is showing signs of fatigue. Welfare, once a decisive advantage, is now facing diminishing returns as voter aspirations evolve. There is a growing emphasis on economic growth, job creation and opportunities beyond state support.    This creates a structural challenge for the Left. Its strengths lie in redistribution and state intervention, but the political conversation is increasingly centred on development and private sector-led growth. Bridging that gap has proved difficult.    At the same time, Kerala’s political landscape is becoming more complex. While traditionally bipolar, the emergence of a third force, even without major electoral breakthroughs, has made contests less predictable. This fragmentation has intensified pressure on both major alliances, particularly the LDF, which must now defend its base while navigating a more competitive environment.    The Congress-led opposition, on the other hand, has shown renewed cohesion, capitalising on anti-incumbency and local grievances.    Congress MP Shashi Tharoor reflected this shift, saying, “I think right now we have got enough contenders. What matters now is that there should be a change of government, a change of policy and a revival of Kerala… making Kerala once again a haven for investment, so that we can grow, generate jobs for our people and prevent a situation where our young people are fleeing the state because they feel they have no possibilities…”    The decline of Left parties in states like West Bengal and Tripura had already reshaped the national opposition landscape. Kerala remains their last major stronghold, both symbolically and politically.    This positions the Congress as the 'first among equals' within the INDIA bloc.

articles.title: West Bengal election results 2026: Trends show BJP doubles tally in seats with over 5% SIR deletions of...
articles.snippet: The TMC may effectively lose half of its seats in these constituencies in the current trends, while the BJP has doubled its tally.
articles.author: Rewati Karan
articles.description: The TMC may effectively lose half of its seats in these constituencies in the current trends, while the BJP has doubled its tally.
articles.body: The 2026 West Bengal Assembly election trends have brought unusual focus to constituencies where more than 5 percent of voters were removed during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.    Data compiled from earlier elections in 2011, 2016, and 2021, along with current trends reported by CNN-News18, shows a dramatic shift in outcomes across these 54 constituencies out of the state’s 293 seats.    2026 trends in high deletion constituencies    In the 2026 trends, among the 54 seats categorised under 'SIR deletions more than 5%', the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is leading in 36 seats, marking a gain of 18 seats compared to previous performance.    The Trinamool Congress alliance (TMC+) is at 18 seats, reflecting a decline of 18 seats. The Congress and others remain at zero in this category, with no change.    These figures stand out because the same group of constituencies previously leaned heavily in favour of the TMC. The swing visible in 2026 trends suggests a major political realignment in these specific areas.    Comparison with 2021 results    In the 2021 West Bengal Assembly election, the same 54 constituencies recorded a very different outcome. The TMC won 36 seats with a vote share of 46.59 percent, while the BJP secured 18 seats with 39.61 percent. The Left alliance did not win any seats but had 10.10 percent of the vote, and others had 3.71 percent without any seats.    This comparison highlights that the TMC may effectively lose half of its seats in these constituencies in the current trends, while the BJP has doubled its tally.    Historical pattern from 2016 and 2011    Looking further back, the 2016 election results show the TMC winning 34 out of these 54 seats with 43.22 percent vote share. The Left alliance secured 17 seats with 38.68 percent, others won 2 seats with 6.95 percent, and the BJP had just 1 seat with 11.15 percent.    In 2011, the TMC had 32 seats with 33.89 percent vote share, while the Left held 14 seats with 44.35 percent. The Congress had 7 seats with 8.36 percent, others had 1 seat with 9.07 percent, and the BJP had no seats, with 4.33 percent vote share.    Over this 15-year period, the BJP’s presence in these constituencies has expanded significantly, culminating in the 2026 trends where it leads the majority.    Scale and impact of SIR deletions    The SIR exercise has been one of the most debated aspects of the 2026 election. Approximately 2.7 million names were removed from West Bengal’s voter rolls, pending adjudication. The electorate size dropped from 7.6 crore to 6.82 crore after the revision.    Across India, the Election Commission conducted SIR in 10 states and three Union Territories, leading to the deletion of 5.58 crore names in total.    In West Bengal specifically, 27.10 lakh electors were deleted under what officials described as “logical discrepancy” criteria, including issues such as spelling errors, surname mismatches, and atypical guardianship records.    The process also involved legal oversight. On the orders of the Supreme Court, 19 appellate tribunals were set up in March to hear appeals. Before the second phase of polling on April 29, tribunals restored voting rights to 1,468 individuals, bringing total reinstatements across two rounds to 1,607.    Only six names were deleted in that phase, taking cumulative removals by tribunals to 14. The restoration-to-deletion ratio stood at 115:1.    Demographic composition of deletions    Data reported by The Hindu indicates that 57.47 lakh of the deleted voters, or 63 percent, were Hindus, while 31.1 lakh, or 34 percent, were Muslims. This is notable because Muslims constitute about 27 percent of the state’s population as per the 2011 census, a figure that incumbent Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee suggested has risen to nearly 33%.    Another figure cited in reports notes that Muslim voters accounted for more than a third of the 90 lakh names removed during the SIR process, making their share of deletions disproportionately high relative to their population share.    Political reactions and competing claims    The role of SIR in shaping the election outcome has been strongly contested. BJP spokesperson GVL Narasimha Rao dismissed claims that voter deletions influenced the results, telling NDTV, &quot;It is not a valid conclusion. If you take the constituencies where there were large SIR deletions and those where there were fewer, the BJP is performing well in both sections. So, saying SIR contributed to the BJP victory would be completely erroneous. It is a motivated conclusion and not based on facts. (sic)&quot;    On the other hand, TMC chief Mamata Banerjee raised serious concerns and refused to concede defeat. She urged party workers to remain vigilant and said, “Just wait and watch,” emphasising that counting was still underway. She also alleged irregularities linked to the electoral process and the SIR exercise.    Turnout and election context    The 2026 election recorded a voter turnout of over 92 percent, the highest since Independence. This is a sharp increase compared to 81.56 percent in 2021 and even surpasses the previous record of 84.33 percent in 2011 — when the TMC won for the first time.    Since 2002, when electoral rolls were digitised, the EC had not carried out an intensive revision, and the SIR marked a departure from its usual practice of updating rolls through annual and pre-election Special Summary Revisions (SSR).    Polling was conducted in two phases: 152 seats voted on April 23 and 142 seats on April 29. Despite the large-scale deletions, turnout increased, setting West Bengal apart from other states where SIR had been implemented.    The data from constituencies with more than 5 percent voter deletions presents a striking narrative. From a TMC-dominated landscape in 2011, 2016, and 2021, these seats have shifted sharply toward the BJP in 2026 trends. While the BJP attributes its performance to broader electoral support, the TMC continues to question the fairness and impact of the SIR process.    With 54 constituencies forming a significant subset of the total 293 seats, their transformation could prove decisive in determining the overall political trajectory of West Bengal.

articles.title: US emerges as India's top LPG supplier in April as Hormuz disruption hits imports
articles.snippet: The US shipped 384,000 tonnes of the cooking fuel followed by Saudi Arabia at 184,000 tonnes, up 42% from the previous month
articles.author: Arunima Bharadwaj
articles.description: The US shipped 384,000 tonnes of the cooking fuel followed by Saudi Arabia at 184,000 tonnes, up 42% from the previous month
articles.body: The US emerged as the largest supplier of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) to India, overtaking traditional Gulf suppliers in April, a month that also saw a drop in imports as the continuing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz hit fuel supplies.    In April, India’s LPG imports dropped to 968,000 tonnes from 1.13 million tonnes in the previous month, ship-tracking data from analytics firm Kpler shows.    The US shipped 384,000 tonnes of the cooking fuel to India against 391,000 tonnes in March.    India has begun sourcing cooking gas from the US to diversify supplies amid the Iran war alongside a long-term deal signed by state-run refiners for 2.2 million tonnes of LPG for 2026, government officials told Moneycontrol requesting anonymity.    The US is the most critical alternative supplier, as it is supported by an established export infrastructure, analysts have said.    Saudi Arabia emerged as the second-largest supplier at 184,000 tonnes, up 41.5 percent from the previous month. Purchases from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) fell 28 percent to 163,000 tonnes.    Before the war broke out on February 28, around 90 percent of India’s LPG imports used to pass through the strait, with India deeply dependent on the Gulf for its energy security.    The West Asia conflict has disrupted the supply chain, forcing India to diversify its imports.    To diversify sourcing and secure cargoes, India ramped up purchases of LPG, primarily a household fuel, from Australia, Chile, and China.    The country bought 22,000 tonnes of LPG from Australia, 13,000 tonnes from Australia and 3,000 tonnes of cooking fuel from China.    While imports from Iran surged nearly six-fold to 63,000 tonnes, those from Qatar dropped 59 percent to 87,000 tonnes.    A Marshall Islands-flagged LPG carrier, MT Sarv Shakti, carrying 46,313 MT of LPG, with 20 crew members, including 18 Indians, safely crossed the Strait of Hormuz on May 2, and is expected to arrive at Visakhapatnam on May 13, data from the shipping ministry shows.    India remains the world's second-largest importer of LPG, with approximately 60 percent of its consumption met through external sources, the bulk of which comes from West Asia. Its annual demand in the range of 30-32 million tonnes, or around 85,000 tonnes a day.

articles.title: 'River Ganga flows to Bengal via Bihar': PM Modi had predicted Bengal win 6 months ago
articles.snippet: Addressing BJP workers after the party’s Bihar sweep in November 2025, PM Modi had said, “The river Ganga flows to Bengal via Bihar… the victory in Bihar, like the river, has paved the way for our victory in Bengal.”
articles.author: Deblina Halder
articles.description: Addressing BJP workers after the party’s Bihar sweep in November 2025, PM Modi had said, “The river Ganga flows to Bengal via Bihar… the victory in Bihar, like the river, has paved the way for our victory in Bengal.”
articles.body: Early counting trends in the West Bengal Assembly elections, on Monday, showed the BJP taking a strong lead over the TMC, with party leaders framing the performance as a continuation of its electoral momentum from Bihar.    Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s earlier political remark linking the Bihar victory to Bengal has resurfaced in the context of the trends. Addressing BJP workers after the party’s Bihar sweep in November 2025, PM Modi had said, “The river Ganga flows to Bengal via Bihar… the victory in Bihar, like the river, has paved the way for our victory in Bengal.”    As counting progressed, the BJP was ahead in 189 seats of the 293 Assembly constituencies, while the TMC was leading in 97, according to Election Commission data. The performance placed the party above the majority mark in early trends, signalling a potential political shift in the state.    Reacting to the developments, BJP supporters gathered outside Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee’s Kalighat residence, raising slogans of “Jai Shri Ram” as counting continued across the state.    The TMC, however, maintained that results were still unfolding, even as BJP leaders projected confidence. Leader of the Opposition Suvendu Adhikari said, “BJP will form the government. People have given the BJP a clear mandate.”    State BJP president Samik Bhattacharya also claimed a decisive win, saying, “People of the state have already rejected the Trinamool Congress government… in the fight between Mamata Banerjee and the people, people have rejected Mamata Banerjee.”    BJP candidates and leaders across constituencies echoed similar sentiment, with party leaders asserting that the results reflected public support for change and for Prime Minister Modi’s leadership. “This victory will inspire our workers in the south too,” PM Modi had said during his Bihar victory speech, a remark now being cited by party leaders as evidence of expanding electoral momentum.    The BJP also appeared to be making strong inroads in Matua-dominated constituencies across North 24 Parganas, Nadia and South 24 Parganas, regions seen as politically crucial with an estimated 40-50 seats.    In several key constituencies, BJP candidates were ahead, including Subrata Thakur in Gaighata and others in Ranaghat Uttar Purba and Ranaghat Dakshin, while TMC candidate Soham Chakraborty led in Karimpur.    The election also triggered sharp political messaging from BJP leaders, with Suvendu Adhikari asserting that the outcome reflected consolidation of Hindu votes. “Hindus could not be divided in the name of language, religion and caste,” he said.    Amid the unfolding trends, Prime Minister Narendra Modi was scheduled to visit the BJP headquarters in New Delhi at 6 pm and is expected to address party workers, according to BJP chief spokesperson Anil Baluni.    In parallel trends from other states, BJP-led alliances were also ahead in Assam, where Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma’s party was leading in 74 of 126 seats, while Puducherry showed a closer contest between Congress, BJP, and AINRC.    As counting continues, the West Bengal trends are being closely watched for signs of a wider national political shift, with the BJP projecting the results as an extension of its Bihar victory narrative and organisational expansion into eastern India.

articles.title: Is Vijay the next MGR? How TVK is shaking Tamil Nadu’s political system like never before
articles.snippet: Drawing comparisons with MGR’s rise, TVK's strong debut signals a potential political reset, though its long-term impact will depend on how it translates momentum into governance.
articles.author: Abhinav Gupta
articles.description: Drawing comparisons with MGR’s rise, TVK's strong debut signals a potential political reset, though its long-term impact will depend on how it translates momentum into governance.
articles.body: Tamil Nadu has always blurred the line between cinema and politics.
