From CN Annadurai to MG Ramachandran and J Jayalalithaa, the state has repeatedly turned cultural icons into political power centres. But what is unfolding now feels different. This is not just another actor stepping into politics. It looks increasingly like a moment that could alter the structure of power itself.    As counting trends unfold, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, led by Vijay, is not merely competing but leading. There is a clear distinction, and it significantly matters. Tamil Nadu’s politics has been dominated by the DMK and AIADMK for nearly six decades. For a debutant party to break into that space and challenge both at once is rare. For it to potentially lead the race is almost unprecedented.    This is why Vijay’s rise needs to be seen through two lenses at once. On one level, it is the story of an actor searching for a meaningful political role, and on another, it is the story of a system being disrupted by a new force.    A political entry years in the making    Vijay’s move into politics was not impulsive. For years, he built a grassroots network through his fan clubs, which gradually evolved into the Vijay Makkal Iyakkam. What began as a social service platform slowly acquired political shape, with local-level mobilisation and electoral participation in smaller contests.    When he formally launched TVK in 2024, the messaging was deliberate. “Politics is not just another profession for me. It is a sacred service of the people,” he said. “Politics is not my hobby, it is my quest.”    Even his films had begun preparing the ground. Over time, his screen persona shifted from pure entertainment to roles that spoke about governance failures, corruption, social justice and public welfare. By the time he entered politics, much of his audience already saw him through a political lens.    A debut that echoes India’s biggest disruptors    Indian politics has seen only a handful of debut moments that changed the game instantly.    When MG Ramachandran launched the AIADMK in 1977, it swept to power and redefined Tamil Nadu’s political structure. When NT Rama Rao founded the Telugu Desam Party in 1983, it delivered one of the most dominant first-time victories in Indian history. Later, the Biju Janata Dal quickly became the central political force in Odisha.    TVK’s current performance places it within that rare category. These moments are not just about seat counts. They signal something deeper. A collapse of established political binaries. A leader whose personal appeal translates into votes. A consolidation of public frustration into a new political channel.    What's unfolding with the poll results on May 4 suggests that Tamil Nadu may be witnessing exactly that.    Why voters are ready for change    The roots of this shift lie in voter sentiment. There is clear fatigue with the DMK-AIADMK cycle. For decades, power has alternated between the two, creating a sense of predictability. While both parties have strong organisational structures and welfare records, many voters now see them as part of an entrenched system.    At the same time, a generational shift is underway. Younger voters, less tied to legacy loyalties, are more open to alternatives. Vijay’s appeal cuts strongly across this group, combining familiarity with the promise of change.    His campaign has also been sharply targeted. TVK’s focus on youth, women and fisherfolk, along with promises around education loans, welfare support and economic relief, has helped it build a broader coalition of voters beyond just fan support.    The limits of charisma    Yet, disruption comes with risks. Tamil Nadu has seen actor-politicians struggle before. Kamal Haasan and Vijayakanth both entered politics with momentum but found it difficult to convert that into sustained electoral dominance.    Vijay faces similar questions. Popularity can open the door, but governance requires depth. Administrative experience, policy clarity and organisational strength will determine whether TVK can sustain its rise.    There have already been warning signs. Incidents like the Karur rally stampede raised concerns about organisational preparedness. Personal controversies have also added scrutiny at a critical moment.    From contender to centre of gravity    Even if TVK falls short of a full majority, its position ensures it will be central to government formation. That alone marks a decisive shift in Tamil Nadu’s politics.    For decades, outcomes were shaped by two poles. Now, a third force is not just relevant but potentially dominant.    This is where Vijay’s journey becomes larger than himself. He is no longer just an actor entering politics. He is the face of a moment that could redefine how power is contested in the state.    An event that could shape the future    History shows that such disruptions rarely remain one-off events. When new forces successfully challenge entrenched systems, they often go on to define politics for years.    Whether TVK follows that path will depend on what comes next. Can it build a durable organisation? Can it translate messaging into governance? Can it move from momentum to stability?    For now, one thing is clear. Vijay’s political journey has moved beyond intent. It has become an event that is already reshaping Tamil Nadu’s political landscape.

articles.title: Syama Prasad Mookerjee: How BJP's 'mission Bengal' was fueled by an 'inseparable link'
articles.snippet: Mookerjee began his political career with the Congress but later moved into independent politics and became associated with the Hindu Mahasabha. Over time, he emerged as a prominent national voice, especially during the turbulent years around Partition.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Mookerjee began his political career with the Congress but later moved into independent politics and became associated with the Hindu Mahasabha. Over time, he emerged as a prominent national voice, especially during the turbulent years around Partition.
articles.body: Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP's) performance in West Bengal is not only a moment of reckoning for the saffron party, but also a moment that two Hindutva stalwarts -- Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Jana Sangh founder Syama Prasad Mookerjee, would have been proud of.    The inability of BJP to cover ground in Bengal, until recently, was something that always bothered the late Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, as Bengal is home to Syama Prasad Mookerjee - an ideologue who played a significant role in the birth of BJP.    With leads consolidating in the northeastern state, the saffron party is currently leading in 188 seats and the Trinamool Congress in 88 seats, according to the Election Commission. As the gap between the two parties widen and clearly indicate an emphatic victory in West Bengal, Bengal's connection with Syama Prasad Mookerjee is back to the fore.    The saffron party's victory in West Bengal will mark the culmination of a long and arduous process that began in 2016. The Party had won 3 seats in 2016 Assembly polls, but kickstarted a process that will form the basis of its consolidation in the all-important north-eastern state. The next assembly polls, in 2021, the BJP managed to secure 77 seats, a significant markup from its previous performance in 2016. The gap between the BJP and TMC was 10 percent in terms of voteshare.    It is no coincidence that an arterial road in South Kolkata is named after the Jana Sangh founder -- Syama Prasad Mookerjee. It is also an indication of resident's familiarity with his name and recognition of Bengal's contribution to the national discourse and the growth of 'nationalist' politics.    The road joins key areas of the city -- ironically, including Kalighat and Bhabanipur, where Trinamool chief Mamata Banerjee's home and her constituency are located.    Today, with Bengal awash with saffron wave , it is perhaps a timely reintroduction to the early 20th Century lawyer, educationist and minister in Jawaharlal Nehru government, who was also the founder of Bharatiya Jan Sangh -- the body precursor to the BJP.    Mookerjee began his political career with the Congress but later moved into independent politics and became associated with the Hindu Mahasabha. Over time, he emerged as a prominent national voice, especially during the turbulent years around Partition.    He also served as Minister for Industry and Supply in the cabinet of Jawaharlal Nehru but resigned in 1950 over differences on the Nehru-Liaquat Pact and broader policy issues, including Kashmir and minority rights.    Union Home Minister Amit Shah, at a rally last month, invoked Mookerjee’s legacy while campaigning in Bengal, calling the state the birthplace of the party’s founding vision.    “This is the land of Ashutosh Mukherjee, who had earned the moniker ‘Tiger of Bengal’. His son, Syama Prasad Mookerjee, founded our party and sacrificed his life for the nation. I pay my respects to both leaders,&quot; Shah had said.    In 1951, he founded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh with support from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). The party emerged as one of the earliest challengers to Congress dominance in independent India and later evolved into today’s BJP.

articles.title: TMC vs BJP: Who dominated West Bengal's north and south regions
articles.snippet: The election is being closely watched as a test for Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, who is seeking a fourth consecutive term.
articles.author: Rewati Karan
articles.description: The election is being closely watched as a test for Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, who is seeking a fourth consecutive term.
articles.body: The ongoing counting of votes for West Bengal’s 293 assembly seats has revealed a stark regional contrast between North and South Bengal, with early trends and historical data indicating a major political shift.    According to figures compiled from CNN-News18 trends and past election data, the contest between the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the All India Trinamool Congress (TMC) is unfolding very differently across the two regions.    North Bengal: Consolidation towards BJP    In North Bengal, which accounts for 54 out of 293 seats, the BJP appears to have significantly strengthened its position. The 2026 trends show the BJP leading in 43 seats, marking a gain of 13 seats compared to earlier performance. The TMC+ alliance is down to 11 seats, reflecting a decline by 12 seats, while Congress remains at zero and others have slipped to zero from one (-1).    This represents a continuation of the BJP’s rise in the region over the past decade. In 2021, the BJP had already secured 30 seats in North Bengal with a 42.74% vote share, while TMC held 23 seats with 45.01%.    Earlier, in 2016, the region was more fragmented, with TMC and Left+ tied at 24 seats each, and BJP marginal at just 2 seats despite a 14.48% vote share. Going further back to 2011, BJP had no presence, while Congress (17), Left (16), and TMC (16) were evenly spread.    South Bengal: Dramatic turnaround    South Bengal, comprising 238 seats in 2026 trends (239 in previous cycles), shows a far more dramatic shift. The BJP is leading in 150 seats, an extraordinary increase of 103 seats, while TMC alliance has dropped sharply to 82 seats, losing by 108. Others account for 6 seats (up by 5), while Congress remains at zero.    This marks a reversal from 2021, when TMC dominated South Bengal with 191 seats and a 49.31% vote share, compared to BJP’s 47 seats and 37.42%. In 2016, TMC had already established strong control with 186 seats, while Left+ held 52 and BJP just 1. In 2011, TMC led with 167 seats, followed by Left at 44 and Congress at 25, with BJP again at zero.    Statewide trends and counting updates    As counting began at 8 am, early data from the Election Commission of India and television reports indicated a tight contest. By 1.30 pm, BJP was ahead in 192 seats, while TMC was leading in 94. Projections from news channels suggested BJP ahead on 195 seats, surpassing the halfway mark of 148 by 39 seats, with TMC at 92.    The election is being closely watched as a test for Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, who is seeking a fourth consecutive term. Responding to early trends, she urged party workers not to panic, stating, &quot;Don't lose hope...we will fight the elections like tiger cubs.&quot; She also alleged that early leads were part of a strategy, claiming, &quot;They are using central forces to harm TMC workers. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) was used to steal votes.&quot;    BJP cites anti-incumbency, says Hindus consolidated    On the other side, BJP leader Suvendu Adhikari expressed strong confidence. &quot;BJP is forming the Government. Initial trends show BJP as 135 plus and approx 100 to TMC,&quot; he said, while acknowledging that some seats like Bhabanipur could be close in early rounds.    Adhikari pointed to shifting voter patterns, saying, &quot;There is anti-incumbency, plus Hindus are consolidated in favour of the Lotus.&quot; He also noted &quot;a Muslim vote bifurcation, especially in Malda, Mushidabad and Uttar Dinajpur.&quot;    Turnout and broader significance    The election also recorded exceptionally high participation, with Phase-II turnout at 91.66% and Phase-I at 93.19%, bringing the combined turnout to 92.47%.    With counting still underway, the final outcome will not only determine the state government but also act as a broader indicator of the BJP’s expansion in eastern India, while the TMC fights to retain its dominance.

articles.title: 35 Bengal seats gear up for photo finish with margins of under 1,000 votes
articles.snippet: In Cooch Behar (732 votes), Sitai (893) and Kalchini (949), the margins remained within striking distance, reflecting intense competition.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: In Cooch Behar (732 votes), Sitai (893) and Kalchini (949), the margins remained within striking distance, reflecting intense competition.
articles.body: The BJP has stormed Mamata Banerjee’s West Bengal bastion, crossing the majority mark and effectively ending the Trinamool Congress’s (TMC) 15-year dominance in the state.    According to current trends, as many as 35 constituencies have been decided by margins of less than 1,000 votes, underscoring how tightly contested the race has been on the ground, as per a Moneycontrol analysis.    From north to south Bengal, several seats witnessed nail-biting finishes. In Cooch Behar (732 votes), Sitai (893) and Kalchini (949), the margins remained within striking distance, reflecting intense competition. The trend continued in seats like Tapan (408), Nabagram (195) and Khargram (572), where candidates were separated by just a few hundred votes.    Some of the closest contests came down to double digits. Naihati saw a stunning margin of just 7 votes, while Mangalokot (23 votes) and Manbazar (21 votes) also recorded razor-thin victories, underlining how every single vote counted in this election.    In the Hooghly and Howrah belt, constituencies such as Uttarpara (527), Serampore (193), Chandannagar (922) and Bally (636) saw tight finishes, while Uluberia Purba (947) and Bagnan (293) added to the list of closely fought seats.    The battleground extended to key political flashpoints like Nandigram (662 votes), along with    Narayangarh (488), Pingla (135) and Keshpur (953) in Paschim Medinipur, all recording narrow victory margins.    Further, constituencies including Bardhaman (705), Memari (162), Purbasthali (546) and Ausgram (761) in Purba Bardhaman, along with Dubrajpur (979), Labhpur (289) and Rampurhat (475) in Birbhum, also witnessed closely fought contests.    The 2026 election was widely viewed as a direct contest betweenBanerjee and the BJP’s state leadership led by Suvendu Adhikari.  Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah drove the party’s campaign strategy.    The West Bengal Assembly has 294 seats. To form the government, a simple majority of 148 seats is needed.    In 2021, Trinamool won 215 seats while the BJP  ended up bagging 77 seats, becoming the main opposition party for the first time in the state assembly.    A victory forBJP  in West Bengal would carry major political and strategic significance, both within the state and nationally.    First, it would mark the end of a long-standing political stronghold by defeatingBanerjee and bringing an end to the All India Trinamool Congress’s prolonged rule.    Second, it would represent a major expansion for the BJP into eastern India—a region where the party has historically struggled to gain dominance. Securing Bengal would solidify its presence beyond its traditional strongholds.    At the national level, a win would significantly boost the leadership of PM Modi reinforcing the party’s electoral momentum and strengthening its position ahead of future elections.

articles.title: How BJP gave a jolt to Mamata in Bengal: 5 reasons behind its victory
articles.snippet: A major factor behind the BJP’s showing in the 2026 West Bengal polls is its targeted outreach to women voters
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: A major factor behind the BJP’s showing in the 2026 West Bengal polls is its targeted outreach to women voters
articles.body: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has gained a significant lead over the TMC in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections, according to the latest trends. The BJP is currently ahead in 186 seats, while the TMC leads in 93.    Counting is still in progress for 293 of the total 294 Assembly constituencies, with more clarity to come in the later part of the day.    A combination of factors helped the BJP deliver a strong performance in the state, where the TMC has been in power for 15 years. Here’s an overview of some of the key drivers --    BJP’s women-centric pitch    A major factor behind the BJP’s showing in the 2026 West Bengal polls is its targeted outreach to women voters. The party attacked the TMC government led by Mamata Banerjee over women’s safety, citing incidents like Sandeshkhali and the RG Kar case to question law and order.    It reinforced this narrative by fielding symbolic candidates linked to these issues (Ratna Debnath in Panihati, Rekha Patra in Hingalganj) and promising higher financial support -- Rs 3,000 per month -- along with stronger safety measures. Leaders including Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Amit Shah emphasised dignity and security for women.    By combining welfare promises with a strong safety narrative, the BJP aimed to dent TMC’s support among women voters, a crucial electoral bloc, helping boost its performance.    Booth-level focus and central push helped narrow gap    The BJP strengthened its grassroots presence in the 2026 West Bengal polls through intensive booth-level management and micro-targeting. Using models like panna pramukhs and shakti kendras, the party expanded voter outreach and tightened organisation on the ground.    Leaders including Amit Shah pushed for sustained local engagement, while membership drives and additional workers helped fill gaps.    Though the TMC retained an edge in rural areas, the BJP’s improved ground network made the contest far more competitive.    Tapping into anti-incumbency, law &amp;amp; order concerns    A major driver of the BJP’s performance in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly polls was its ability to capitalise on anti-incumbency against the government led by Mamata Banerjee. The party framed the election around issues of corruption, unemployment, and governance fatigue after 15 years of TMC rule.    Law and order became the emotional core of its campaign, with incidents like Sandeshkhali and the RG Kar case used to highlight alleged failures in policing and women’s safety.    By combining this narrative with promises of stricter governance and better welfare support, the BJP was able to convert public discontent into votes, contributing to its strong showing.    Infiltration central to BJP’s core messaging    The BJP made cross-border infiltration a central campaign issue, framing it as a threat to local identity, resources, and security. The party accused the government led by Mamata Banerjee of enabling illegal immigration for vote-bank politics.    PM Modi, Amit Shah, and other leaders promised stricter border control and action against illegal immigrants, while also reaching out to refugee communities with citizenship assurances. “I want to assure the people of West Bengal, form a BJP government with a full majority, we will act decisively under the policy of ‘detect, delete and deport’, and remove all infiltrators from Bengal,” said Shah during one of his campaigns.    Combined with other issues, it played a key role in strengthening the BJP’s position in the closely contested election.    Countering ‘outsider’ tag    The BJP actively worked to counter the TMC’s “outsider” narrative, which portrayed it as a Delhi-driven party. To respond, the BJP projected itself as rooted in Bengal’s culture and identity.    A key part of this strategy was the “son of the soil” pitch by Amit Shah, who repeatedly said the next chief minister would be a Bengali-born leader familiar with the state’s language and culture. Local leaders like Suvendu Adhikari were prominently showcased in this framing.    The party also leaned heavily on cultural symbolism. PM Modi and other leaders frequently invoked “Jai Maa Durga” and “Jai Maa Kali” at rallies, blending Hindutva messaging with Bengali religious identity to connect with voters.    Alongside this, the BJP highlighted local issues, promoted state leaders, and participated in Bengali festivals to reinforce its “Bengal-first” image.

articles.title: From 1967 to 2026: Disruption isn't new in Tamil Nadu politics, but is Vijay's TVK rewriting the playbook?
articles.snippet: Tamil Nadu’s first major disruption came in 1967, when the DMK defeated the Congress, ending its long rule since Independence.
articles.author: Manisha Lal Khandpur
articles.description: Tamil Nadu’s first major disruption came in 1967, when the DMK defeated the Congress, ending its long rule since Independence.
articles.body: Actor-turned politician Vijay's Tamilaga Vetri Kazhagam (TVK) has emerged as a 'massive disruptor' in its electoral debut in Tamil Nadu politics this year, according to initial trends shown by the Election Commission of India. His party is likely to emerge as the single largest party in the state, dealing a strong blow to ruling DMK. But, when we look back at the state's history, there have been several such shocks that changed power equations, voter behaviour and political narratives.    Here's a deep dive in Tamil Nadu politics and the disruptions that have shaped it over several decades.    1967: The original political earthquake    Tamil Nadu’s first major disruption came in 1967, when the DMK defeated the Congress, ending its long rule since Independence. The disruption was led by C. N. Annadurai and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) rode on anti-Hindi protests, food shortages and a strong regional identity wave.    This election witnessed the first reset in Tamil Nadu politics as it became highly dominated by Dravidian parties.    1972–1977: Rise of MGR and creation of a second pole    Five years on, the next big reset came from within the DMK. Film star M. G. Ramachandran (MGR), who stepped into politics in 1953 by joining DMK split from the party in 1972 and launched AIADMK. By 1977, he had swept to power, turning Tamil Nadu into a two-party system—DMK vs AIADMK. This was not just disruption; it created a new permanent power centre. For any actor entering politics today, MGR remains the benchmark.    1989: Instability after MGR    After MGR passed away 1987, AIADMK split into factions, leading to political instability. The instability opened doors for DMK to return to power in 1989, under the leadership of M. Karunanidhi.    2006 &amp;amp; 2011: The rise and fall of a third force    Actor-turned politician Vijayakanth's DMDK made an electoral debut bringing a new kind of disruption. Even though in 2006 state assembly election, the party managed to win just one seat but it brought damage to DMK and AIADMK by cutting their vote share. It secured around 8–10% vote share. In the history of Tamil Nadu elections, for the first time, it witnessed a hung assembly with no party gaining majority. However,  In 2011, in alliance with AIADMK, DMDK won 29 seats and became the Opposition.    But the rise was short-lived. By 2016, DMDK failed to win a single seat and gradually faded.    The Pattern: Third fronts rise, then fade    Over the years, several parties like PMK, NTK, MNM, AMMK have tried to break the DMK-AIADMK dominance. Many touched 3–10% vote share and influenced results in specific seats.    Yet, the larger picture barely changed. The two main Dravidian parties still control the bulk of votes.    2026: TVK as the new disruptor    This brings us to 2026. Vijay’s TVK has energised young and urban voters, positioning itself as a party of “change”. Early projections suggest TVK could secure around 19–24% vote share. TVK’s strategy echoes past disruptors. Like DMK in 1967, it taps into a desire for change. Like MGR and Vijayakanth, it relies heavily on a charismatic film star.    Moment or movement?    Tamil Nadu has historically allowed only two types of long-term disruptors- strong ideological movements like DMK, or mass leaders like MGR who built deep party structures. TVK now stands at a crossroads. Its 2026 performance may shake up vote shares and alliances. But what happens after that will decide its future.

articles.title: BJP set to make history in West Bengal: Who are CM frontrunners
articles.snippet: Unlike in some other states, the BJP has not officially declared a chief ministerial face in West Bengal. However, with the party heading towards a decisive victory, several leaders are now being discussed as potential contenders.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Unlike in some other states, the BJP has not officially declared a chief ministerial face in West Bengal. However, with the party heading towards a decisive victory, several leaders are now being discussed as potential contenders.
articles.body: As early trends indicate a strong surge for the BJP in West Bengal, the spotlight has shifted to who could become the state’s next Chief Minister. The party is leading on nearly 200 seats, while the TMC appears to be trailing around the 100-seat mark.    Unlike in some other states, the BJP has not officially declared a chief ministerial face in West Bengal. However, with the party heading towards a decisive victory, several leaders are now being discussed as potential contenders based on their political standing and organisational influence.    Here are the likely contenders in for CM post.    Suvendu Adhikari    Suvendu Adhikari is currently the most prominent BJP face in West Bengal politics and the Leader of Opposition in the state Assembly. His political significance stems from his strong organisational base in districts like East Midnapore and his ability to mobilise support in key constituencies. He was once a close aide of Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee in the Trinamool Congress and held influential ministerial positions in the state government. However, ahead of the 2021 Assembly elections, he broke away from the TMC and joined the BJP, marking one of the most high-profile political exits in recent Bengal politics. The fallout between Suvendu Adhikari and Mamata Banerjee remains one of the most defining rivalries in the state’s political landscape, with both leaders frequently engaging in sharp political confrontation. This direct challenge to Mamata’s leadership is a key reason why Suvendu is widely seen as the BJP’s most viable Chief Ministerial face in Bengal.    Dilip Ghosh    Dilip Ghosh is a senior BJP leader and former state president who played a major role in expanding the party’s presence in West Bengal. During his tenure, the BJP significantly strengthened its organisational structure and emerged as a strong opposition force, particularly in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections. Known for his aggressive political style and grassroots outreach, he remains an influential veteran figure in the party despite no longer holding the state presidency.    Shamik Bhattacharya    Shamik Bhattacharya, the current West Bengal BJP president, represents the organisational leadership of the party in the state. His focus is largely on internal restructuring, booth-level management, and election strategy. He is considered more of a strategist and administrator rather than a mass electoral face.    Agnimitra Paul    Agnimitra Paul, BJP MLA from Asansol South and national spokesperson, is an emerging leader in the party’s Bengal unit. A former fashion designer, she has built visibility through national media appearances and is often projected as part of the BJP’s effort to promote women leadership in the state. While not a top CM contender, she is considered a rising political voice.    Shankar Ghosh    Shankar Ghosh, BJP MLA from Siliguri, is an important regional leader from North Bengal. He has been active in local mobilisation and organisational work in the region. His influence is more regional than statewide, but he is part of the broader leadership group being watched for future roles within the party.

articles.title: PM Modi to visit BJP headquarters this evening after poll results; likely to address party workers
articles.snippet: Exuding confidence about forming the next government in West Bengal, BJP leaders said people of the state have voted for change and in favour of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Exuding confidence about forming the next government in West Bengal, BJP leaders said people of the state have voted for change and in favour of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
articles.body: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit the BJP headquarters in New Delhi on Monday evening as early trends pointed to significant gains for the party in West Bengal and Assam.    The prime minister is also expected to address party workers at the BJP headquarters, continuing a pattern seen during previous election victories. “Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji will visit BJP HQ, New Delhi today at 6 PM,” BJP chief spokesperson Anil Baluni said in a post on X.    Besides West Bengal and Assam, the NDA is also likely to retain power in Puducherry. The BJP was forging a possible victory path in West Bengal with leads in 178 seats against the ruling TMC’s 92 and surging ahead in Assam, while actor-politician Vijay’s TVK was set for a stunning debut in Tamil Nadu, ahead in 105 seats, leaving the ruling DMK in the third position, according to trends on the Election Commission website.    As votes were counted for assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, the east seemed set to be coloured a vivid saffron. In Kerala, the Congress was ahead in 59 seats, the CPM in 29 and the CPI in nine.    Exuding confidence about forming the next government in West Bengal, BJP leaders said people of the state have voted for change and in favour of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.    The BJP was leading in 171 seats against the TMC's 83 as counting progressed for 293 assembly segments, signalling a political shift in the state.    Leader of the Opposition Suvendu Adhikari asserted that the BJP will form the next government in the state.    Adhikari is seeking re-election from Nandigram and taking on Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee in Bhabanipur.    “BJP will form the government. People have given the BJP a clear mandate,” Adhikari told reporters.    Maintaining that Muslim voters have not gone en masse with the TMC in this election, he claimed that Hindu votes, on the other hand, have consolidated in favour of the BJP.    “Hindus could not be divided in the name of language, religion and caste,” he said.    Adhikari said it will be a victory of PM Modi, who led the BJP's campaign in the state.    “All Hindus have united in favour of PM Modi,” he said.    State BJP president Samik Bhattacharya said he was confident of a landslide victory for the party.    “People of the state have already rejected the Trinamool Congress government, and in a few hours, the overwhelming majority of the seats will confirm that in the fight between Mamata Banerjee and the people, people have rejected Mamata Banerjee,” Bhattacharya said outside a counting centre in Kolkata.    BJP's Kharagpur Sadar candidate Dilip Ghosh claimed that people have voted for change.    “The counting will be conducted in the same manner as the polling. People have voted to bring a new government,” he told PTI Videos.    BJP's Noapara candidate Arjun Singh said the election will blaze the trail for change.    “We firmly believe, with full confidence and trust, that this change will happen and the BJP will win the elections,” he said.    BJP's Gaighata candidate Subrata Thakur said his party will get more than 180 seats.    “With Prime Minister Narendra Modi guiding us from Delhi, we will form a double-engine government. In past elections, there were strong-arm tactics. This year the EC ensured free and fair polls. People have voted for 'poriborton',” he said.    BJP leader Sishir Bajoria said his party will make a clean sweep in the elections.    “Have you heard anything from Didi's (CM Mamata Banerjee) side? They have fallen silent,” he said.    BJP's Darjeeling MP Raju Bista said the verdict showed those who supported infiltrators, corruption, and could not stop violence against women have been rejected by people.    “This victory also paid tribute to the 100 of BJP workers who sacrificed their lives under TMC terror,” he said.    *With Agency Inputs

articles.title: India’s wheat exports restart after 4-year pause; ITC ships cargo as global buyers test prices
articles.snippet: First shipment to UAE signals India’s return to global wheat trade, though higher domestic prices may limit large-scale exports.
articles.author: Reuters
articles.description: First shipment to UAE signals India’s return to global wheat trade, though higher domestic prices may limit large-scale exports.
articles.body: Indian traders have begun exporting wheat for the first time in four years, as ample stocks, higher global prices and firmer freight rates have opened a window for them to make small shipments to buyers in Asia and the Middle East, trade sources said.    Consumer goods conglomerate ITC has started loading 22,000 metric tons of wheat at the western port of Kandla for shipment to the United Arab Emirates, sources said, declining to be identified as they were not authorised to speak to the media.    ITC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.    India, the world's largest wheat producer after China, has allowed exports of the grain this year, lifting a ban on overseas sales imposed in 2022.    New Delhi extended curbs in 2023 and 2024 after extreme heat shrivelled crops and depleted stocks, pushing domestic prices to record highs and fuelling speculation it might need to import wheat for the first time since 2017.    Last year's favourable weather led to a robust harvest, quashing speculation about imports, helping the government rebuild depleted reserves and giving it the confidence to allow exports.    Earlier this year, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government allowed traders to export 2.5 million tons of wheat, before permitting another 2.5 million tons late last month for shipments.    Despite the permission to export, lower global prices and higher Indian rates dissuaded traders from signing export deals.    But the Iran conflict has pushed up freight costs and some buyers who need immediate shipments have turned to India, the trade sources said.    The deal to export 22,000 tons of wheat to the United Arab Emirates was signed at around $275 per ton free on board, sources said.    Despite the first export deal in four years, India is unlikely to see a surge in wheat exports, as domestic prices have risen in recent days because of crop damage, making Indian wheat more expensive than rival supplies from Australia or the Black Sea region.    Australian and Black Sea supplies are priced at around $290-$300 per ton, including cost, insurance and freight, leaving Indian wheat at least $20 a ton more expensive in global markets.    Only buyers with immediate supply gaps are likely to turn to Indian wheat, while those with adequate inventories of Australian, Argentine or Black Sea supplies will find it less attractive given its relatively higher prices, the sources said.    Importers with urgent, short-term requirements and seeking shipments within 30-45 days are the most likely to buy Indian wheat, they said.

articles.title: Tamil Nadu election 2026: What TVK means as Vijay’s party surges in debut polls
articles.snippet: As per trends, TVK has disrupted the state’s traditional bipolar contest.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: As per trends, TVK has disrupted the state’s traditional bipolar contest.
articles.body: The meaning and intent behind the name of Vijay’s political outfit, Tamil Nadu Vetri Kazhagam (TVK), has come into focus as the party records a strong showing in early trends of the 2026 Tamil Nadu Assembly elections.    According to material published by the party’s IT wing on its website, the name “reflects the fundamental purpose of our party and our commitment to the society,” adding that it “defines our determination to achieve success through the welfare of the people.”    The three components -- Tamil Nadu, Vetri, and Kazhagam, which means Tamil Nadu Victory Party -- are presented as a structured articulation of its ideology.    The first element points to identity and geography. The party explains that &quot;Tamil Nadu&quot; or &quot;Tamilakam&quot; represents &quot;the people of Tamil Nadu, which is the core of our work, and the pride of our culture&quot;.    The second component, Vetri, meaning victory, signals ambition. As described, “Victory reflects our desire to always achieve and our mission to bring about change for society,” with a stated focus on “social justice, equality, and fairness.”    The final term, Kazhagam, frames the party as a collective. It “defines us as a social service organisation with a united and integrated approach,” highlighting coordinated efforts by members and volunteers.    In a more detailed note, the party reiterates that “each part of this name has been chosen to portray the vision of progress, unity, and success of Tamil Nadu and its people.” It adds that Kazhagam “means ‘organisation’ or ‘unity,’” underscoring collective action for development.    This ideological framing comes alongside a striking electoral debut. Early trends indicate TVK leading in over 100 seats in the 234-member assembly, with the majority mark at 118. As per the current Election Commission trends, Vijay's party is ahead in 104 seats while AIADMK is leading in 64. DMK is lagging with leads in just 47 seats.    News channels show that TVK is ahead in over 109 seats, while AIADMK is leading in 60. The ruling DMK is leading in over 43 seats. While it's still too early to call the election, trends indicate a strong debut by Vijay, who banked heavily on his popularity to woo the voters in the state.    Contesting independently, TVK has disrupted the state’s traditional bipolar contest. With no pre-poll alliance, its performance raises the likelihood of post-result negotiations in the event of a hung assembly, potentially positioning Vijay as a central figure in government formation.

articles.title: Kerala’s ‘Captain’ faltering: Did Pinarayi Vijayan’s 2021 magic fade too fast?
articles.snippet: Vijayan's LDF turned the rotating table trend in 2021, but seems to have faltered to create the same magic in 2026 Assembly elections.
articles.author: Chhabi Kala
articles.description: Vijayan's LDF turned the rotating table trend in 2021, but seems to have faltered to create the same magic in 2026 Assembly elections.
articles.body: &quot;This election has changed the tradition of experiments, which is why this is historic...&quot; said Pinarayi Vijayan when his party emerged victorious for the second consecutive term in 2021 Kerala Assembly elections.    Traditionally, Kerala never elects a ruling party to power. After every five-year term, the state ends up choosing an alternative front (between the Left Democratic Front, LDF or the United Democratic Front, UDF). The last time when there was a departure from this pattern was four decades ago.    But LDF bucked that trend in 2021. Vijayan rose to victory for the second time as he steered the state through a sea of crises - 2018 and 2019 floods, Nipah virus outbreak, cyclone Ockhi and the Covid pandemic.    He was pitched as the man who transformed Kerala.    The LDF won 99 out of 140 Assembly seats, eight seats more than what it won in 2016, made it a historic victory for Vijayan, considering the LDF campaign revolved almost entirely around the Chief Minister.    On bucking anti-incumbency, Vijayan had said, “The state had a tradition of experimenting with governments every alternate election. This election has changed that, which is why this is historic.”    For 2026 Kerala Assembly elections, the LDF campaign projected Vijayan as ‘captain’, a strategy that seems to have worked for the LDF so far. On reels and roadside banners, the CPI(M)’s poll slogan read, “if not LDF, then who?”    However, the current Election Commission trends show that the 'Captain' factor has likely failed to deliver results as per the party expectations.    According to the Election Commission data, trends show a lead for Congress-led UDF on nearly 100 of the 140 seats.    The Ramesh Chennithala-led Congress opposition once again raised the anti-incumbency factor this time. The biggest arnesal of all was the Sabarimala issue. The Vijayan government's handling of the highly sensitive subject was criticised heavily by the UDF.

articles.title: Who is Abdul Rasheed, man giving tough fight to Pinarayi Vijayan as Congress eyes last Left-ruled state
articles.snippet: Pinarayi Vijayan, who has served two consecutive terms as Chief Minister of Kerala and led the only Left Democratic Front (LDF)-ruled state in the country, is facing a tough contest in Dharmadom as early counting trends show a close fight with Congress candidate V. P. Abdul Rasheed.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Pinarayi Vijayan, who has served two consecutive terms as Chief Minister of Kerala and led the only Left Democratic Front (LDF)-ruled state in the country, is facing a tough contest in Dharmadom as early counting trends show a close fight with Congress candidate V. P. Abdul Rasheed.
articles.body: Pinarayi Vijayan, who has served two consecutive terms as Chief Minister of Kerala and led the only Left Democratic Front (LDF)-ruled state in the country, is getting tough fight in the Dharmadom constituency according to early counting trends.    Vijayan, who first assumed office on May 25, 2016 and was sworn in again on May 20, 2021, becoming the first Chief Minister of Kerala to be re-elected after completing a full five-year term, is now leading with 1,536 votes after earlier trailing Congress candidate V. P. Abdul Rasheed following the completion of the seventh round of counting out of 15 rounds.    In early trends, the Indian National Congress (INC) is leading with 60 seats, while the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI(M)) is ahead in 27 and the Communist Party of India (CPI) is leading in 10 seats.    Who is Abdul Rasheed?    Abdul Rasheed was initially expected to contest from Taliparamba, but a reshuffle within the United Democratic Front (UDF) led to him being fielded in Dharmadom. He had earlier reduced the LDF’s margin significantly in Taliparamba in the 2016 Assembly elections, contesting against CPM state secretary M. V. Govindan. In 2021, his candidature again narrowed the LDF’s lead, while in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections the UDF performed strongly in the constituency, winning a majority of booths.    Political background of Pinarayi Vijayan    Born in 1944 in Kannur district’s Pinarayi village, Vijayan rose from a humble background as the 14th child in his family. He joined the CPI(M) at the age of 24 and became part of the district committee early in his political career.    He entered electoral politics in 1970, winning from Kuthuparamba, a seat he retained in subsequent elections with increasing margins. Over the years, he held key positions within the party, serving as state secretary from 1998 to 2015 and joining the CPI(M) politburo in 2002, a position he continues to hold.

articles.title: Tamil Nadu stares at a hung house: Three possible ways Vijay’s TVK could still form the govt
articles.snippet: Tamil Nadu Election Results 2026: TVK is leading in Tamil Nadu but may fall just short of the majority mark, making government formation dependent on post-poll alliances.
articles.author: Abhinav Gupta
articles.description: Tamil Nadu Election Results 2026: TVK is leading in Tamil Nadu but may fall just short of the majority mark, making government formation dependent on post-poll alliances.
articles.body: Counting trends in the Tamil Nadu Assembly elections suggest that Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, led by Vijay, is in a strong position but may still fall short of a clear majority. Current trends show TVK hovering around 110 to 112 seats in the 234-member House, with the AIADMK bloc at around 68 seats and the DMK alliance close to 55.    The majority mark stands at 118. That means Vijay could end up just a few seats short, forcing him to look at post-poll arrangements. If the numbers do not change significantly, three broad paths could shape the next government, as noted by CNN-News18.    Option 1: Building support from smaller parties    One route for TVK is to reach out to smaller parties that have won a handful of seats. These include players like the Congress, PMK, CPI and VCK.    This option allows Vijay to remain firmly in control of the government without sharing space with a major rival. It would also help him preserve his political messaging as an alternative to both the DMK and AIADMK.    However, this path comes with its own complications. Smaller parties often seek important ministries and a role in decision-making. Managing multiple partners could make governance slower and more complex, especially for a first-time administration.    Option 2: A tie-up with AIADMK for stability    The second and more straightforward option is a post-poll alliance with the AIADMK, which is currently the second-largest bloc.    A TVK-AIADMK partnership would comfortably cross the majority mark and provide a stable government. AIADMK leaders, particularly Edappadi K. Palaniswami, bring administrative experience that could support Vijay’s transition into governance.    But this option is politically sensitive. Vijay has positioned himself as a break from the old Dravidian order. Aligning with AIADMK could dilute that image. There is also the question of the Bharatiya Janata Party, which has been associated with AIADMK in recent years. Any indirect linkage could create discomfort among TVK’s support base.    Option 3: An unlikely pivot toward the DMK bloc    The third possibility is the least expected but cannot be ruled out in Indian politics. A deal involving the Congress could open the door for a broader arrangement that includes the DMK.    Such a move would create a strong majority and position the alliance as a larger anti-BJP front at the national level.    However, this would be a difficult political shift. Vijay has directly targeted M. K. Stalin and the DMK during his campaign. Joining hands with them could confuse voters who supported TVK as a clear alternative.    A new phase in Tamil Nadu politics    Regardless of which path is chosen, one thing is certain. Tamil Nadu is entering a new political phase.    If TVK does not reach the majority mark on its own, it will still hold the key to government formation. Vijay will have to move from leading a campaign to managing alliances and expectations.    The final numbers may shift as counting progresses, but the larger picture is already visible. The era of straightforward DMK versus AIADMK contests is giving way to a more complex and competitive political landscape.

articles.title: SEBI to issue advisory on AI risks, investor empowerment next phase for SEBI mandate: Tuhin Kanta Pandey
articles.snippet: Speaking at the IMC Capital Markets conference, SEBI Chair Tuhin Kanta Pandey noted that a growing India needs innovation that solves real problems, reducing friction, widening access, lowering costs, and supporting capital formation
articles.author: Anishaa Kumar
articles.description: Speaking at the IMC Capital Markets conference, SEBI Chair Tuhin Kanta Pandey noted that a growing India needs innovation that solves real problems, reducing friction, widening access, lowering costs, and supporting capital formation
articles.body: SEBI will soon issue an initial advisory on vulnerabilities linked to AI models and AI-led risk detection systems, as a part of the regulator’s growing focus on technology-driven threats in financial markets.    Speaking at the IMC Capital Markets conference, SEBI Chair Tuhin Kanta Pandey noted that a growing India needs innovation that solves real problems, reducing friction, widening access, lowering costs, and supporting capital formation. But while innovation like digital onboarding, faster settlement, direct payout, online bond platforms, REITs, INVITs, AIFs, municipal bonds, green bonds, commodity derivatives show how products and processes can deepen markets, widen access, and improve risk management, innovation also brings risks.    “This is especially relevant as next-generation AI models become more powerful. While these tools can help identify weaknesses faster, they can also exploit vulnerabilities at speed and scale. In an interconnected securities market, a single weak link can create wider risks. Regulated entities have to stay ahead of such risks through stronger cyber resilience, continuous monitoring, and faster remediation,” he said adding that SEBI is in constant touch with market participants and relevant stakeholders as the latest challenge after MYTHOS and similar AI models test our resilience.    While investor protection will always remain central to SEBI's mandate, Pandey added that the next phase for SEBI is investor empowerment. “Protection prevents harm. Empowerment builds capability. India has seen a sharp rise in investor participation through mutual funds, digital platforms, and young investors entering the market. This is positive, but participation must be responsible. Access must be matched with awareness. Choice must be matched with suitability.    &quot;We have engaged with all stakeholders on this and shortly we are going to issue an advisory in terms of how they should really be doing very alert on the vulnerabilities that may be there and doing a proactive role in trying to do that,&quot; Pandey said.    Convenience must be matched with caution. Investor education must therefore be simple, practical, and continuous. Risks, costs, incentives, and grievance mechanisms must be explained clearly and upfront. Investor empowerment must also include protection from fraud. Investors must know who is regulated, how to verify an intermediary etc,” he added.    Pandey further noted that in an interconnected securities ecosystem, weaknesses in one segment can ripple across the system. SEBI, he added, is in constant engagement with market participants to address such risks collaboratively.

articles.title: West Bengal elections 2026: TMC faces erosion in Muslim-dominated seats as trends hint at BJP gains
articles.snippet: This marks a clear departure from the 2021 Assembly elections, where TMC swept 43 out of 44 Muslim-majority seats with a vote share of 57.96%, leaving BJP with zero seats despite securing 21.68% votes.
articles.author: Rewati Karan
articles.description: This marks a clear departure from the 2021 Assembly elections, where TMC swept 43 out of 44 Muslim-majority seats with a vote share of 57.96%, leaving BJP with zero seats despite securing 21.68% votes.
articles.body: Early counting trends in West Bengal’s 2026 Assembly election indicate that the Trinamool Congress (TMC) is no longer holding the same level of dominance in Muslim-majority constituencies as seen in previous elections.    Out of 293 seats, 43 constituencies with over 50% Muslim population are currently showing a changed picture. According to trends, TMC+ is ahead in 30 seats, reflecting a drop of 12 compared to earlier performance, according to CNN-News18. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), on the other hand, is leading in 9 such seats, marking a gain, while others account for 4 seats, up by 3.    This marks a clear departure from the 2021 Assembly elections, where TMC swept 43 out of 44 Muslim-majority seats with a vote share of 57.96%, leaving BJP with zero seats despite securing 21.68% votes. The Left and other parties were also marginal players then.    Historical context and voting patterns    The current shifts stand out sharply against past trends. As per CNN-News18 data bank, in 2016, Left+ had secured 26 of these seats with 47.17% vote share, while TMC won 18. Going further back to 2011, the political landscape was more fragmented: Congress won 18 seats, TMC 12, Left 12, and others 2.    Since 2011, however, Muslim voters have largely consolidated behind Mamata Banerjee and her party, playing a decisive role in her repeated electoral successes. This consolidation followed dissatisfaction with Left Front policies and was reinforced by socio-economic concerns highlighted in the 2006 Sachar Committee findings.    Demographic weight and electoral importance    Muslims constitute around 27% of West Bengal’s population as per the 2011 Census, a figure that Banerjee has suggested has risen to nearly 33%. Their influence spans roughly 85 constituencies with over 30% Muslim population and 112 seats where their share exceeds 25%.    Districts such as Murshidabad (over 66% Muslim population), Malda, and Uttar Dinajpur remain crucial. In 2021, TMC dominated Murshidabad by winning 20 of 22 seats. However, recent developments suggest volatility. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise led to 4,55,137 voter deletions in Murshidabad and 2,39,375 in Malda, while approximately 12,400 voters were added on average in Muslim-dominated seats.    Turnout has also surged significantly, with increases ranging from 2 to 20 percentage points across 85 such constituencies. Malda recorded particularly sharp rises: 16.2 points in Ratua, 15.3 in Chanchal, 14.7 in Malatipur, and 14.1 in Habibpur.    Signs of fragmentation and counter-consolidation    BJP leader Suvendu Adhikari has attributed the party’s improved performance as per trends to a combination of Hindu consolidation and a split in Muslim voting. He stated, “This time there's a Hindu consolidation, and the way Muslims vote for TMC, they have not done that this time. Some votes have gone to the pro-Muslim party. BJP has also got some in small amounts.”    Highlighting booth-level trends, he said, “In the first round, out of 14 booths, six are Muslim-dominated booths where the TMC earlier secured 90–95% votes. This time, they have not got that level of support. There is a crack.”    He further added, “There has been a Muslim bifurcation… the kind of 90–95% consolidation seen in 2021 and 2024 is no longer there.”    Broader political implications    Adhikari also linked the BJP’s gains to national leadership, saying the “guarantee” of Prime Minister Narendra Modi has resonated with voters. He projected that the BJP could reach “135 plus” seats, though he cautioned that these are early trends based on initial rounds and postal ballots.    While TMC continues to lead in a majority of Muslim-dominated constituencies, the erosion in its margins and emerging competition signal a potentially significant shift in West Bengal’s electoral dynamics

articles.title: End of six decades of Dravidian duopoly? Why TN voters looked beyond DMK and AIADMK to Vijay's TVK
articles.snippet: Tamil Nadu Election Results 2026: This is not just an electoral upset in the making. It reflects a growing impatience with a political system that has been dominated by the same two parties since 1967.
articles.author: Abhinav Gupta
articles.description: Tamil Nadu Election Results 2026: This is not just an electoral upset in the making. It reflects a growing impatience with a political system that has been dominated by the same two parties since 1967.
articles.body: Early trends in the Tamil Nadu Assembly elections are pointing to more than just a strong performance by Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), led by actor-turned-politician Vijay. They are signalling a deeper churn in voter behaviour. Led by Vijay, TVK is ahead in over 100 seats in both television projections and Election Commission data, comfortably outpacing both the AIADMK alliance and the ruling DMK alliance.    This is not just an electoral upset in the making. It reflects a growing impatience with a political system that has been dominated by the same two parties since 1967. The scale of TVK’s rise suggests that a significant section of voters has actively chosen to move away from the DMK-AIADMK binary, raising a larger question: why are Tamil Nadu voters looking beyond the parties that have defined its politics for decades?    Voter fatigue with a decades-old duopoly    The most obvious reason is fatigue. For nearly six decades, power has alternated between two Dravidian giants. While both parties have delivered on welfare and identity politics, many voters now see them as part of an entrenched system that has grown predictable.    Reports suggest that this election became a referendum not just on governance but on the lack of alternatives. TVK has tapped into this sentiment by positioning itself as a break from the familiar cycle.    A generation looking for something new    There is also a generational shift underway. Younger voters, many of whom do not carry the historical loyalty to Dravidian parties, appear more willing to experiment.    Vijay’s appeal cuts strongly across this demographic. His popularity as a film star gives him immediate recognition, but what seems to have worked is how he has channelled that into a political narrative about change and accountability.    According to a report by Deccan Chronicle, the “TVK wave” is not confined to one region. It has shown traction even in urban constituencies and traditional DMK strongholds like Chennai.    Anti-incumbency against the DMK    The ruling DMK, led by MK Stalin, entered the election with a governance record built around welfare schemes and what it described as the “Dravidian model.”    However, anti-incumbency appears to have played a role. Concerns over rising costs, employment opportunities, and local governance issues have created dissatisfaction in sections of the electorate. The gap between welfare delivery and economic aspirations seems to have widened, particularly among urban and middle-class voters.    AIADMK’s inability to reclaim space    At the same time, the AIADMK has struggled to present itself as a strong alternative. Internal divisions, leadership questions after the era of J. Jayalalithaa, and a lack of a compelling narrative have weakened its position.    As a result, a large share of anti-DMK votes appears to have shifted not to the AIADMK, but to TVK, which is seen as a fresher option.    The power of a simple message    TVK’s messaging has been direct and emotive. It has leaned heavily on anti-establishment sentiment and the idea of clean governance. While critics argue that the party’s policy framework remains underdeveloped, voters seem to have responded to its clarity of intent.    Vijay’s campaign often referenced moments like 1967 and 1977, when political upheavals reshaped the state. That framing appears to have resonated with voters who see this election as another such turning point.    Can momentum translate into power?    Even if TVK does not cross the majority mark, its current position ensures that it will play a decisive role in government formation. In a fragmented verdict, it could emerge as the kingmaker, shaping alliances and policy direction.    That possibility itself marks a shift. For the first time in decades, the DMK-AIADMK binary is no longer guaranteed to determine the outcome.    A political reset in motion    Tamil Nadu’s electorate is sending a strong message. It is not just voting for a party, but expressing a desire for change. Whether TVK can convert this surge into stable governance remains an open question. Popularity and momentum can win elections, but governing a complex state requires organisation, policy depth and experience.    For now, however, one conclusion stands. The old order is being challenged, and Tamil Nadu’s politics may not look the same again.

articles.title: RG Kar to Durgapur: Is Mamata's formidable votebank behind her decimation in Bengal? Here's what results...
articles.snippet: Leading upto the polls, the impact of the recent violence against women on the TMC electoral prospects was being widely discussed as women voters form a primary constituent in Mamata's overall electoral calculus.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Leading upto the polls, the impact of the recent violence against women on the TMC electoral prospects was being widely discussed as women voters form a primary constituent in Mamata's overall electoral calculus.
articles.body: As leads begin to solidify in West Bengal indicating a decisive victory for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), recent incidents of violence against women in West Bengal is back as major talking points with political pundits discussing the electoral outcome in the eastern state threadbare.    The Trinamool Congress, according to Election Commission's recent update is leading in 70 seats and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is leading in 117 seats. However, all major television channels, according to early leads, have given the BJP a decisive mandate with more than 150 seats.    There are 39 seats in which women voters outweigh male voters. Out of these 39 seats, BJP is leading on 29 seats and the TMC is leading on 10.    Leading upto the polls, the impact of the recent violence against women on the TMC electoral prospects was being widely discussed as women voters form a primary constituent in Mamata's overall electoral calculus.    The most recent alleged gang rape of a second-year student of a private medical college in Durgapur in October 2025 once again highlighted the rise of violence against women in the eastern state.    The crime took place just four months after a first-year student of a government-run law college in south Kolkata was gang-raped inside the college premises, and 14 months after the rape and murder of a trainee doctor inside R.G. Kar Medical College and Hospital in August 2024. These incidents had once again raised questions about women’s safety in West Bengal and the state’s claim of being one of the safest places for women.    Leading upto the polls, the Bharatiya Janata Party has consistently attacked Mamata Banerjee-led TMC government over crime against women in the. In a recent interview, days ahead of counting, BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra said, the entire country is deeply saddened by the horrific incident of rape in a law college in Kolkata.    He said, it is heartbreaking that such brutal crimes against women are repeatedly emerging from Bengal, a state where a woman serves as the Chief Minister. Patra alleged that the victim’s statement suggests that it appears to be state-sponsored brutality. He also said, the main accused Manojit Mishra has reportedly been the secretary of the TMC’s student wing.    In 2013, the Trinamool government launched Kanyashree. Similar to a 1994 programme in Bangladesh, it was aimed at preventing child marriage by providing cash incentives to girls studying in school. In 2015, the West Bengal government started a bicycle distribution scheme called Sabooj Sathi with a focus on schoolgirls, providing them a safe way to travel to school.    Both schemes proved to be extremely popular, resulting in the school dropout rates among girls falling to half that of boys. Driven partly by this, from 2018-’20, Bengal ranked first in decline of dropout rate amongst all the states in the Indian Union.    In 2016, the Trinamool reaped the benefit of this women-centric welfare with as many as 52% of its votes coming from women, as per CSDS-Lokniti survey data, as it swept the election. In 2019, faced with an ascendent BJP, this came down marginally to 51%. But even then the Trinamool was pulling in far more female votes than any other party: 47% of Bengal’s women voted Trinamool while only 38% went with the BJP.

articles.title: Welfare schemes that proved gamechangers in India's 2026 assembly elections: A state-wise analysis
articles.snippet: From Tamil Nadu's Rs 13,807 crore women's cash transfer to Assam's 40-lakh beneficiary Orunodoi: How five governments made welfare their ballot strategy
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: From Tamil Nadu's Rs 13,807 crore women's cash transfer to Assam's 40-lakh beneficiary Orunodoi: How five governments made welfare their ballot strategy
articles.body: India's 2026 assembly elections, spanning Tamil Nadu, Kerala, West Bengal, Assam, and Puducherry, were a test of whether voters prefer state welfare programmes or other political alternatives, with nearly 25 crore people casting their votes across the four states and one union territory. Across all five contests, welfare schemes occupied the centre of every party's campaign, manifesto, and voter outreach. Below is a state-by-state, scheme-by-scheme account of the programmes at the heart of the 2026 electoral cycle.    Tamil Nadu    Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thittam (KMUT)    The Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thittam is the DMK government's flagship monthly cash transfer scheme for women. It currently benefits 1.31 crore women across Tamil Nadu, with a 2025-26 budget allocation of Rs 13,807 crore, providing Rs 1,000 monthly to female heads of households.    Ahead of the poll announcement, the Tamil Nadu government transferred Rs 5,000 to 1.31 crore women beneficiaries in February 2026, comprising Rs 3,000 as an advance for three months and a Rs 2,000 'special summer assistance.' The DMK's election manifesto committed to enhancing the monthly amount to Rs 2,000.    The scheme was named 'Magalir Urimai Thogai,' meaning a 'rightful entitlement,' as a deliberate framing choice, positioning the cash transfer as a legitimate demand from the state rather than a government dole.    Free bus travel for women    The second flagship intervention was free bus travel for women, described as a scheme that fundamentally expanded the geography of work and care, allowing women to access employment and services without the financial burden of transit costs.    The Dravidian welfare framework    Tamil Nadu's welfare measures are framed within its long-standing Dravidian model of social justice delivery. DMK spokesperson Dr. Kanimozhi NVN Somu stated: &quot;The electoral dividends are visible in the raw data. This engagement is not a sudden epiphany of the digital age but is rooted in a decades-long evolution that began with the fundamental politics of nutrition.&quot; Women's workforce participation in Tamil Nadu stands at over 40 per cent, one of the highest in the country.    West Bengal    Lakshmir Bhandar    Lakshmir Bhandar is the TMC government's flagship welfare scheme, providing monthly financial assistance to women from economically weaker sections. The programme has been a central pillar of the party's grassroots strategy and has been widely credited with strengthening the TMC's presence in rural regions of the state.    In the 2026 campaign, the TMC leveraged Lakshmir Bhandar as an electoral shield, presenting it alongside the party's broader development record and governance continuity as the principal reasons for re-election.    BJP's counter-scheme: Rs 3,000 monthly for women    The BJP, in its 'Sankalp Patra' manifesto, promised Rs 3,000 per month in financial assistance for women, significantly higher than the amount provided under the existing TMC scheme. Exit poll data pointed to a potential 10 per cent swing in women's votes towards the BJP.    Assam    Orunodoi    Orunodoi is the BJP government's flagship direct benefit transfer (DBT) scheme in Assam. Under the programme, eligible women receive monthly financial assistance of Rs 1,250 directly into their bank accounts. The scheme currently covers nearly 40 lakh beneficiaries across the state.    In a large pre-election disbursement, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma transferred Rs 9,000 to four million women on March 10, 2026, a total outlay of Rs 3,600 crore, described as the largest such disbursement in the state's history, including a three-month bonus to mark the Bihu festival.    The BJP's Sankalp Patra pledged to increase monthly assistance under Orunodoi to Rs 3,000 in phases, expand coverage to an additional 15 lakh households, and provide a Rs 25,000 lump sum to existing beneficiaries. Sarma also announced that two women from the same household would be eligible, relaxing the existing one-family-one-beneficiary rule.    With roughly 75 per cent of Assam's population touched by at least one state scheme, Orunodoi created what analysts describe as a loyal 'labharthi' class of beneficiaries. Exit polls credited the programme as a decisive factor in voter sentiment.    Mukhyamantri Mahila Udyamita Abhiyan (MMUA)    The Mukhyamantri Mahila Udyamita Abhiyan provides an entrepreneurial fund for rural women to support small businesses. The BJP manifesto pledged to create 40 lakh 'Lakhpati Baideos,' women entrepreneurs crossing the Rs 1 lakh annual income mark, through livelihood and entrepreneurship support linked to the scheme.    Mukhyamantri Nijut Moina and Nijut Babu Asoni    The Mukhyamantri Nijut Moina scheme provides monthly student assistance to girl students, Rs 1,000 to those in Class 11, Rs 1,250 to undergraduates, and Rs 2,500 to postgraduate students, paid for 10 months in a year through DBT. Its male counterpart, the Mukhyamantri Nijut Babu Asoni, launched in February 2026, provides Rs 1,000 per month to first-year male undergraduates and ₹2,000 to postgraduate students from families earning below Rs 4 lakh annually.    Kerala    Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhathi (KASP)    The Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhathi is the LDF government's health insurance scheme. During its second term, the Pinarayi Vijayan government spent Rs 4,236.22 crore under KASP, providing free medical treatment up to Rs 5 lakh to nearly 1.5 crore people from 42.1 lakh families across Kerala.    Welfare Pensions    The LDF government spent Rs 48,383.83 crore on welfare pensions during its second term, ensuring timely monthly payments of Rs 2,000 to 62 lakh beneficiaries. The 2026 LDF manifesto proposed increasing this pension to Rs 3,000 per month.    LIFE Mission (Housing)    Under the LIFE Mission, the LDF government provided houses to 4.81 lakh families, with the total expected to cross 5.25 lakh by the end of the second Pinarayi Vijayan term.    UDF's Counter-Welfare Proposals    The Congress-led UDF's manifesto promised 'No Bill' hospitals modelled on the Puducherry-based JIPMER framework, free dialysis, and an Oommen Chandy Health Insurance Scheme providing Rs 25 lakh health coverage per household. The UDF also committed to reviving the Karunya Benevolent Fund.    Fiscal Context    The LDF government stated that the average annual expenditure during the five years of its second term was Rs 1,69,547 crore, compared to Rs 1,17,191 crore during the first Pinarayi Vijayan government and Rs 68,028 crore during the Oommen Chandy government from 2011 to 2016. The state's outstanding debt-to-GSDP ratio declined to approximately 33 to 34 per cent in 2025-26, down from over 38 per cent in 2021.    Puducherry    Monthly Financial Assistance for Women    The AINRC-BJP NDA government under Chief Minister N. Rangasamy provided Rs 2,500 in monthly financial assistance to women heads of families. Rangasamy stated that while the scheme currently covers 73,000 women, he committed to expanding coverage to all eligible women with no ceiling if the alliance is re-elected.    Old-Age Pensions and Government Employment    The Rangasamy government raised old-age pensions to up to Rs 4,000 per month and filled approximately 5,000 vacant government positions during the current term.    Public Distribution System (PDS)    The government revived the Public Distribution System to ensure direct home delivery of rice to beneficiaries, 10 kg for yellow-type priority households and 20 kg for red category, high-priority households. A Rs 3,000 cash gift was also distributed to 3.47 lakh ration card holder families.

articles.title: The league that never loses: IUML is quietly having its best Kerala election in 15 years
articles.snippet: Leading in 23 of 27 seats contested, IUML is on course for its best kerala assembly performance in 15 years, and a bigger voice in the next government
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Leading in 23 of 27 seats contested, IUML is on course for its best kerala assembly performance in 15 years, and a bigger voice in the next government
articles.body: As the United Democratic Front heads for a decisive victory in the 2026 Kerala Legislative Assembly election, one of the most significant sub-stories of counting day is the performance of its longest-standing partner, the Indian Union Muslim League.    On current official ECI trends, the IUML is leading in 23 of the 27 seats it contested. That puts it on course to become the third largest single party in the 140-member Kerala assembly, ahead of the CPI, which leads in 10 seats, and every other party in the house. Only the INC at 61 and the CPI(M) at 28 are ahead of it in individual party standings.    The numbers become more striking when context is added. The CPI(M), leading in 28 seats, has contested nearly five times as many constituencies as the IUML. The League's strike rate on current trends stands at over 85 percent of its contested seats.    If the leads hold through to formal declaration, it would be the IUML's best assembly performance since its record 20-seat haul in 2011, and a significant improvement over its 15-seat tally in 2021.    IUML constituency-wise snapshot: Where the League stands    Across the 23 constituencies where the IUML is currently leading, the margins tell a story of a party performing with consistency across its geographic base.    The largest leads are in Vallikunnu, where T.V. Ibrahim leads by 19,411 votes, Mankada where Manjalamkuzhi Ali leads by 17,360, and Malappuram where P.K. Kunhalikutty leads by 16,203.    Strong five-figure margins are also recorded in Ernad (12,888), Perinthalmanna (11,626), Mannarkkad (12,899), Manjeshwar (10,288), and Tanur (10,360). The party's leads are spread across Kasaragod, Kozhikode, Malappuram, Palakkad, Thrissur, Ernakulam, and Kannur districts, reflecting the geographic breadth the IUML has built beyond its Malappuram heartland.    Three constituencies remain closely contested: Kasaragod, where Kallatra Mahin leads by 841 votes, Guruvayoor where C.H. Rasheed leads by 624, and Kalamassery where Adv. V.E. Abdul Gafoor leads by 2,497, all still in early-to-mid counting rounds.    Notably, Adv. Fathima Thahiliya, one of two women candidates fielded by the IUML for the first time in its history, is leading in Perambra by 5,289 votes.    Seven decades of structural consistency    The IUML was formed on March 10, 1948 in Madras, now Chennai, as the Indian successor to the All-India Muslim League following Partition. It adopted its current name and constitution on September 1, 1951, positioning itself firmly within India's constitutional framework from its inception.    From as early as 1952, the IUML has had representation in the Indian Parliament. In Kerala, it has functioned as a community-based party that has operated almost exclusively through democratic coalition politics, aligning consistently with the Congress-led UDF since the front's formation.    The party has increased its seat count in the Kerala Legislative Assembly from 14 seats in 1982 to 20 seats in 2011. That 2011 figure, 20 out of 23 seats contested, remains the party's best-ever Kerala assembly result. Today's trends suggest 2026 may rival or surpass it.    The 2026 campaign    For the 2026 election, the IUML contested 27 seats, with state president Panakkad Sadiqali Shihab Thangal releasing the candidate list and highlighting a conscious effort to bring in younger faces and increase representation for women, fielding two women candidates for the first time in the party's history.    Senior leader P.K. Kunhalikutty was shifted to contest from Malappuram, while K.M. Shaji was fielded from Vengara. Kunhalikutty, a former Union Minister and the League's most senior electoral face, is currently leading in Malappuram by over 5,000 votes, one of the largest individual margins in the district today.    Malappuram: The fortress holds    In Malappuram, the IUML's primary base and the district where it wields the most consistent influence, early trends show the party leading across the majority of constituencies. The League is also leading strongly in Kozhikode, Palakkad, and Kannur districts, reflecting its geographic spread across Kerala's Malabar region.    What the third-place standing means    The IUML's position as the third largest party in the assembly, if trends hold, carries practical significance beyond the symbolism. In a UDF government, the League's seat count directly determines its share of cabinet portfolios and its weight in coalition negotiations. A 23-seat IUML, up from 15 in 2021, would enter government formation discussions with considerably more leverage than it held going into the last UDF government in 2016, when it won 18 seats.    &amp;nbsp;

articles.title: Who is Vijay’s astrologer who predicted a 'tsunami victory' and CM post
articles.snippet: Pandit, known for his bold and often controversial predictions, grabbed fresh attention after being seen visiting Vijay’s residence with a bouquet and a ceremonial shawl.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Pandit, known for his bold and often controversial predictions, grabbed fresh attention after being seen visiting Vijay’s residence with a bouquet and a ceremonial shawl.
articles.body: Celebrity astrologer Radhan Pandit has suddenly found himself back in the spotlight as early election signals boost Vijay and his party, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), in Tamil Nadu.    Pandit, known for his bold and often controversial predictions, grabbed fresh attention after being seen visiting Vijay’s residence with a bouquet and a ceremonial shawl.    He had earlier described Vijay’s horoscope as “extraordinary”, even calling it a “tsunami horoscope”, and claimed that the actor-politician would rise to the top, potentially becoming chief minister with a dominant vote share. According to Pandit, Vijay’s planetary alignment sets him apart from his rivals.
