articles.body: The counting of votes for the 2026 state elections across four key states and one Union Territory will begin at 8 am on May 4.    Kerala, Assam and Puducherry went to the polls in a single phase on April 9, while Tamil Nadu voted on April 23. West Bengal, witnessing a fierce contest between the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress and the BJP, saw polling in two phases on April 23 and 29.    The counting process will start with postal ballots, followed by votes recorded in Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs).    The Election Commission, which conducts the polls, divides each assembly constituency into multiple rounds. In every round, a fixed number of EVMs are counted, with results shared with representatives of all political parties.    To ensure transparency and accuracy, EVM results are cross-verified with VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) slips.    Tight security    Counting centres are secured under a three-tier system. In a first, the Election Commission has introduced QR code-based Photo Identity Cards through ECINET to prevent unauthorised entry.    In West Bengal, the poll body has deployed 165 additional counting observers and 77 police observers, along with strict access controls, including a ban on mobile phones except for returning officers and authorised observers.    What exit polls say    Mamata Banerjee is aiming for a fourth consecutive term against a strong BJP challenge, while the CPI(M) and Congress are seeking to regain lost ground after their rout in 2021. Smaller players, including Humayun Kabir’s AJUP and Asaduddin Owaisi’s AIMIM, are also in the fray in select pockets. Most exit polls give an edge to the BJP, with few predicting a comfortable win for the TMC.    In Tamil Nadu, pollsters largely expect the MK Stalin-led DMK to return to power, though a few predict a surprise win for TVK. In Kerala, the contest is seen as tight between the Congress-led UDF and the CPI(M)-led LDF. In Assam, Himanta Biswa Sarma is widely expected to retain power against Gaurav Gogoi’s challenge, while in Puducherry, the BJP-led NDA is likely to consolidate its position.    With agency inputs

articles.title: AI translation goof-up? Himachal textbook misprints ‘Kinnaur’ as ‘Kinner’, to issue corrigendum
articles.snippet: The error was spotted in the English version of Folk Culture of Himachal and Yoga book, according to a Times of India report.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: The error was spotted in the English version of Folk Culture of Himachal and Yoga book, according to a Times of India report.
articles.body: In a major goof-up, Kinnaur- a mountainous district located in Himachal Pradesh was wrongly translated as 'kinner' (transgender) in class 6 textbook of the Himachal  Pradesh Board of School Education.    The error was spotted in the English version of Folk Culture of Himachal and Yoga book, according to a Times of India report.    Following this, the Himachal Pradesh Board of School Education has said it would issue a corrigendum to correct the wrongly translated word, the report added.    Quoting a board officials, the report said that the error likely occurred during translation from Hindi to English as the Hindi version of the book carried the correct name. The official further added that it could be possible that the translation was done using an AI tool that read 'Kinnaur' as 'Kinner' meaning transgender.    However, board secretary said the translation work was assigned to an expert, it is unclear the error was AI generated or manual.    The issue also rekindles earlier sensitivities surrounding the term &quot;Kinner&quot;. In 2007, its use in the film Traffic Signal triggered protests in Kinnaur, prompting then chief minister Virbhadra Singh to condemn it and leading to the film being banned in the state.

articles.title: Election Results 2026: Inside counting day, how votes are tallied, verified and declared
articles.snippet: The counting process in each constituency is overseen by a Returning Officer appointed by the Election Commission of India. These officers are nominated in consultation with state governments and are responsible for ensuring that counting is conducted as per the rules.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: The counting process in each constituency is overseen by a Returning Officer appointed by the Election Commission of India. These officers are nominated in consultation with state governments and are responsible for ensuring that counting is conducted as per the rules.
articles.body: The results for assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry will be declared today, May 4, with vote counting set to begin at 8 am.    While outcomes are expected by evening, early trends are likely to emerge by the afternoon, following the standard counting sequence that starts with postal ballots and moves to votes recorded in Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs).    Date and time    Date: May 4  Counting begins: 8 am  Early trends: Expected within the first few hours  Final results: Likely by afternoon or evening    Who conducts the counting    The counting process in each constituency is overseen by a Returning Officer appointed by the Election Commission of India. These officers are nominated in consultation with state governments and are responsible for ensuring that counting is conducted as per the rules.    Where counting takes place    The Returning Officer also decides the counting centre for each constituency, while the schedule is fixed by the Election Commission. Counting is carried out under strict supervision, with each round typically covering votes from 14 EVMs.    How the counting unfolds    Counting staff are selected through a three-stage randomisation process to maintain neutrality. Each table is supervised by a counting supervisor, and micro-observers are deployed to ensure compliance.    Candidates and their authorised agents are present throughout the process.    The counting begins with Electronically Transmitted Postal Ballots (ETPB) and standard postal ballots. EVM counting can begin 30 minutes after postal ballot counting starts, even if all such ballots have not been tallied.    Step-by-step process    Step 1: Postal ballots  Postal ballots are counted first. These include votes from service voters such as armed forces personnel, government officials on duty, and certain categories of senior citizens.    Step 2: EVM counting  EVMs are opened in rounds, with each machine representing a polling station. Votes are displayed on the control unit and recorded. The number of rounds depends on the size of the constituency. Results are declared after each round, shaping the overall trend.    VVPAT verification  To ensure transparency, VVPAT slips from randomly selected polling stations, usually five per constituency, are verified. This acts as a cross-check between electronic results and paper records.    Final declaration  Once all rounds are complete, votes are consolidated, and the candidate with the highest tally is declared elected. The Returning Officer formally announces the result and issues a certificate to the winner.    How to track results  Live, seat-wise updates will be available on the official website of the Election Commission. Users can also track results via the ECINET mobile application.    &amp;nbsp;

articles.title: Assembly elections 2026: What happens if two candidates get the same votes? Here’s how winners are...
articles.snippet: Indian election law has a well-defined and straightforward provision to deal with such scenarios.
articles.author: Ria Kapoor
articles.description: Indian election law has a well-defined and straightforward provision to deal with such scenarios.
articles.body: As counting of votes begins across Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and West Bengal, the focus is naturally on which party or candidate is leading and by what margin.    In most constituencies, results are decided by clear vote differences, sometimes running into big number differences. However, elections can also produce razor-thin margins that keep candidates and voters on edge till the very last round of counting.    In extremely rare cases, the contest can reach a complete deadlock, where two candidates secure exactly the same number of votes.    This raises an obvious question: How does the system decide a winner when there is no numerical difference at all? Is there a re-election, another round of voting, or some other mechanism?    Indian election law has a well-defined and straightforward provision to deal with such scenarios.    According to the guidelines of the Election Commission of India, if two candidates receive an equal number of votes after counting, and even after any recount if conducted, the result is decided by a draw of lots.    This process is conducted by the Returning Officer in the presence of the candidates or their representatives. It works like a lottery.    The candidate whose name is picked is declared the winner. Legally, this is treated as if the candidate has received one additional vote over the opponent.    Before this stage, candidates do have the option to request a recount. If a candidate or their election agent believes there has been an error in counting, they can submit a written application seeking a recount.    However, this request must be supported by valid reasons. The election officer reviews the application and decides whether a recount should be allowed.    Indian election law does not provide for a re-election in the case of a tie. Once the counting and any recount process are completed, the draw of lots becomes the final method to resolve the deadlock.    After the winner is decided, the result is formally announced by the election authorities. A list of winning candidates is then released and published in the official gazette. This ensures the process is documented and legally recognised.    &amp;nbsp;    &amp;nbsp;

articles.title: Mamata Banerjee alleges 'deliberate power cuts', CCTV shutdowns; blames BJP hours before counting

articles.body: Hours before counting begins in one of the most anticipated state elections in recent memory, West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee on Monday alleged that “deliberate load-shedding” was being carried out in parts of the state and urged TMC workers to remain on high alert outside strong rooms where votes are stored.    In a post on X, Banerjee claimed she had received reports from areas including Serampore in Hooghly, Krishnanagar in Nadia, Ausgram in Burdwan, and Kolkata’s Kshudiram Anushilan Kendra, where power cuts were being imposed in phases, CCTV cameras allegedly switched off, and vehicles seen moving in and out of strong room premises.    Hours before the counting of votes, West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee on Monday alleged that “deliberate load-shedding” was being carried out in parts of the state and urged party workers to remain on high alert outside strong rooms where votes are stored.    In a post on X, the West Bengal chief minister claimed she had received reports from areas including Serampore in Hooghly, Krishnanagar in Nadia, Ausgram in Burdwan, and Kolkata’s Kshudiram Anushilan Kendra, where power cuts were being imposed in phases, CCTV cameras allegedly switched off, and vehicles seen moving in and out of strong room premises.    The remarks come hours before the counting of votes begins across the state at 8:00 am with postal ballots, followed by EVM counting at 8:30 am, with results to be updated in real time on ECINET and the official election portal.    Meanwhile, West Bengal Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) Manoj Kumar Agarwal on Sunday also issued a stern warning against disruption, promising a transparent and peaceful counting day backed by a massive security apparatus.    In a series of briefings ahead of the count, Agarwal emphasised that the Election Commission has left nothing to chance, deploying a rigorous three-tier security system to guard counting centres across the state.    To ensure the integrity of the process, a multi-layered force has been mobilised. 200 companies of Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) are dedicated exclusively to counting centres. Security is divided between the State Police, State Armed Police, and CAPF. CCTV cameras have been installed outside counting halls to monitor all movement.

articles.title: West Bengal SIR row sparks job fears as professionals move Calcutta High Court over voter roll deletions
articles.snippet: Among those who have moved the court are a central government PSU officer, a government school teacher, an insurance agent, and a medical aspirant preparing for a national-level entrance exam, as per the report.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Among those who have moved the court are a central government PSU officer, a government school teacher, an insurance agent, and a medical aspirant preparing for a national-level entrance exam, as per the report.
articles.body: A group of working professionals in West Bengal has approached the Calcutta High Court, arguing that the deletion of their names from electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) threatens not just their voting rights but also their livelihoods.    According to the report by The Times of India, the petitions underline anxieties that go beyond disenfranchisement and extend into employment, licensing, and career prospects.    Among those who have moved the court are a central government PSU officer, a government school teacher, an insurance agent, and a medical aspirant preparing for a national-level entrance exam, as per the report. All claim that being removed from voter lists raises doubts about their citizenship status, which could have direct professional consequences.    Justice Krishna Rao, hearing the matter last week, reportedly indicated that the petitions would be taken up later, offering no immediate relief ahead of elections or, in one case, before a crucial examination.    SIR-related deletions have affected around 27 lakh people across the state.    Petitioners have argued that for individuals in regulated professions or government service, absence from electoral rolls can trigger suspicion about their nationality. This, they say, may lead to disciplinary proceedings, loss of employment, or cancellation of professional licences.    One petitioner, a 40-year-old assistant general manager in a PSU from Murshidabad’s Bhagabangola constituency, has been quoted to state that despite being listed in draft rolls published on December 16, he was later summoned over a discrepancy involving his father’s name in older records from 2002.    Although he submitted multiple documents in support of his case, his name did not appear in the final list, and an appeal before the designated tribunal failed.    “The sudden removal of my name from the rolls creates a cloud of suspicion regarding my citizenship, which may... jeopardise my service benefits, or act as a bar to continued employment,” his petition reads, as per the report.    A government school teacher has filed a similar plea. Representing him, counsel told the court on April 28, “SIR had taken a lot from these people, their right to vote being a crucial loss. Now, these people are worried about their jobs and whether this deletion will complicate things in their professional lives,” while requesting urgent consideration of the matter.    The concerns are equally acute in the private sector. A 52-year-old insurance agent from Tehatta in Nadia district moved the court, pointing out that his licence depends on his voter status. His legal counsel emphasised the gravity of the situation, stating, “His position is not merely a source of livelihood but one of public trust... The arbitrary deletion of his name from the electoral rolls directly threatens the validity of his insurance licence and agency appointment.”    For a 32-year-old medical professional from Nadia’s Kaliganj constituency, the stakes are immediate. He is scheduled to appear for the Institute of National Importance Combined Entrance Test conducted by AIIMS Delhi on May 16, for which proof of citizenship is mandatory. While his parents and siblings cleared the SIR process, he did not.    Having completed house staffship at Kolkata’s Sambhunath Pandit Hospital and Chittaranjan Seva Sadan, he is now seeking judicial relief. His plea expresses hope that intervention would “not only restore (his) legal right to vote but also protect (his) career”, the report said.

articles.title: By-Poll Results Live: Vote counting underway in Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Nagaland and Tripur
articles.snippet: The Election Commission of India will begin vote counting for the recent by-elections held in seven legislative constituencies spread across Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Nagaland, and Tripura.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: The Election Commission of India will begin vote counting for the recent by-elections held in seven legislative constituencies spread across Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Nagaland, and Tripura.
articles.body: The Election Commission of India began vote counting for the recent by-elections held in seven legislative constituencies spread across Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Nagaland, and Tripura. The counting process started at 8 AM on May 4, and final results for all seats are scheduled to be declared later today.These bypoll results are being announced in parallel with the much larger assembly election outcomes for major states, including Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Puducherry.Which Seats Are Going to the Polls Today?The by-elections were triggered primarily due to the unfortunate passing of sitting legislators. Here is a breakdown of the constituencies in focus:Umreth, Gujarat: The vacancy arose after the demise of BJP representative Govindbhai Parmar. The ruling party has fielded his son as the candidate, while the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) opted to withdraw from this contest.Bagalkot, Karnataka: This seat fell vacant following the death of former minister H.Y. Meti, who was a member of the Congress party.Davanagere South, Karnataka: The bypoll here was necessitated after the passing of the incumbent Congress MLA, Shamanur Shivashankarappa.Baramati, Maharashtra: Considered a traditional stronghold of the Nationalist Congress Party (NCP), this high-profile seat required a by-election after the demise of former Deputy Chief Minister Ajit Pawar in a January aviation accident.Rahuri, Maharashtra: Voting was held here due to the death of the sitting BJP legislator, Shivaji Kardile.Koridang, Nagaland: The by-election was triggered by the death of the constituency’s BJP MLA, Imkong L. Imchen.Dharmanagar, Tripura: This seat went to a bypoll following the passing of the previous legislator and state Speaker, Biswa Bandhu Sen of the BJP.Note: The scheduled by-election for the Ponda constituency in Goa was cancelled following a directive from the Bombay High Court, which upheld petitions challenging the validity of the election notification.You can monitor real-time updates on Moneycontrol and through the official Election Commission of India portal. The designated webpage—results.eci.gov.in—features a specific section labeled 'Bye Election to Assembly Constituencies: Trends & Results May 2026.' Live data and round-by-round counting trends will be updated continuously through the morning.For the first time in these bypoll counts, election authorities have introduced QR code-based photo identification cards for authorized personnel. Officials confirmed that a three-layered security protocol is in effect at all counting venues to ensure the integrity of the process. These same security and technological arrangements are also being applied to the simultaneous counting for the five state assembly elections.

articles.snippet: The political temperature in Puducherry has been unusually high. Voting was held on April 9, 2026, and the Union Territory witnessed an extraordinary voter engagement of 89.87% — the highest ever recorded in its electoral history.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: The political temperature in Puducherry has been unusually high. Voting was held on April 9, 2026, and the Union Territory witnessed an extraordinary voter engagement of 89.87% — the highest ever recorded in its electoral history.
articles.body: The Union Territory of Puducherry enters a decisive day today as vote counting begins for the 2026 Assembly elections. The counting process will officially commence at 8:00 AM IST across all 30 constituencies of the coastal territory. The Election Commission of India (ECI) has confirmed that the tabulation of postal ballots will be taken up first, followed immediately by the counting of votes recorded in Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs).The political temperature in Puducherry has been unusually high. Voting was held on April 9, 2026, and the Union Territory witnessed an extraordinary voter engagement of 89.87% — the highest ever recorded in its electoral history.This election was widely viewed as a direct contest between two major coalitions:	The Ruling NDA Alliance: Comprising the AINRC, BJP and AIADMK.	The Opposition India Bloc: A united front led by the Congress and DMK.All eyes are on Chief Minister N. Rangaswamy. Having been a dominant figure in Puducherry politics for decades, he now faces the toughest test of his career. Analysts are watching closely to see whether his governance record will outweigh the typical voter fatigue that comes with a party in power for consecutive terms.While the NDA is hoping that local development work and central schemes will shield them from anti-incumbent sentiment, the Congress-DMK alliance has aggressively campaigned on issues like rising living costs and governance lapses.Where to Watch Live ResultsReal-time updates will be available through multiple official channels. Voters and enthusiasts can track the hourly trends via:	The ECI’s Official Website: results.eci.gov.in	The Voter Helpline Mobile App: Developed by the ECI.	The Puducherry State Election Commission’s official portal.	News platforms (such as Moneycontrol) are also providing minute-by-minute live coverage alongside analytical commentary.As the postal ballots are opened and EVM seals are broken this morning, the fate of Puducherry’s next government will begin to crystallize. Stay tuned with Moneycontrol live for the latest updates as the numbers roll in.

articles.title: Promoters turn selective buyers in March quarter after two years of heavy selling
articles.snippet: Among companies witnessing consistent promoter buying over four quarters were Godrej Properties, Chambal Fertilisers and Chemicals, JM Financial, Maharashtra Seamless, Suprajit Engineering, Pilani Investment and Industries, Senco Gold, Raymond Lifestyle, DB Corp, Rashi Peripherals and BL Kashyap and Sons, among others.
articles.author: Moneycontrol News
articles.description: Among companies witnessing consistent promoter buying over four quarters were Godrej Properties, Chambal Fertilisers and Chemicals, JM Financial, Maharashtra Seamless, Suprajit Engineering, Pilani Investment and Industries, Senco Gold, Raymond Lifestyle, DB Corp, Rashi Peripherals and BL Kashyap and Sons, among others.
articles.body: Promoters turned selective buyers in the March quarter, increasing stakes in several companies after sustained selling during 2024 and 2025 amid elevated valuations. Data from ACE Equities showed that out of around 4,700 listed firms, promoters raised their holdings in 695 companies, with 50 of these seeing stake increases for four consecutive quarters.    Among companies witnessing consistent promoter buying over four quarters were Godrej Properties, Chambal Fertilisers and Chemicals, JM Financial, Maharashtra Seamless, Suprajit Engineering, Pilani Investment and Industries, Senco Gold, Raymond Lifestyle, DB Corp, Rashi Peripherals and BL Kashyap and Sons, among others.    On a sequential basis, promoter stake increases were also seen in companies such as Adani Enterprises, GMR Airports, JSW Energy, Grasim Industries, Jindal Stainless, Maruti Suzuki and Indus Towers. These increases were largely concentrated in asset-heavy sectors such as power, infrastructure and real estate.        According to a note by Jefferies, promoter purchases in 2026 have been driven through open market buying, participation in rights issues and acquisitions from strategic investors, with transactions aggregating to over $4 billion. Promoter buying was observed in companies including Godrej Properties, Adani Energy, Maruti, Grasim, Jindal Stainless, Lodha and Indus Towers.    Promoters of Adani Enterprises subscribed to rights issues in proportion to their holdings, investing around $2 billion, while promoters of GMR Airports committed nearly $1 billion through multiple transactions. Additionally, promoters of JSW Energy participated via equity placements and convertible warrants.    The brokerage noted that valuation comfort appears to be a key driver behind the renewed promoter interest. The MSCI India Index has declined about 6 percent so far in 2026, with its one-year forward price-to-earnings multiple easing to around 20.2 times, closer to the 10-year average, compared with a peak of 22 times in earlier periods.    On the other hand, promoter selling continued in several companies. Promoter holdings declined in 467 firms during the quarter, with 109 companies witnessing stake reductions for four consecutive quarters.    Companies where promoters have consistently reduced stakes for four straight quarters include Wipro, SBI Life Insurance, Cholamandalam Investment and Finance, HDFC AMC, Aditya Birla Capital, ICICI Lombard, Oracle Financial Services Software, FSN E-Commerce Ventures, AU Small Finance Bank, Dixon Technologies and Nippon Life India Asset Management, among others.    Over the past two years, promoters have been significant net sellers, with aggregate sales of about $56 billion across 2024 and 2025. Of this, around $36 billion was executed through secondary market block deals, while about $20 billion came via IPOs. This sustained selling has led to a decline in promoter ownership in BSE-500 companies to an all-time low of 48.4 percent as of December 2025.

articles.title: India's top billionaires bounce back from March lows as markets recover
articles.snippet: Indian markets staged a strong comeback in April, with benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty gaining over 6 percent each. The broader markets saw an even sharper rally, with the BSE MidCap 150 index jumping 12.7 percent and the BSE SmallCap 250 index surging 18 percent.
articles.author: Ravindra Sonavane
articles.description: Indian markets staged a strong comeback in April, with benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty gaining over 6 percent each. The broader markets saw an even sharper rally, with the BSE MidCap 150 index jumping 12.7 percent and the BSE SmallCap 250 index surging 18 percent.
articles.body: India's top billionaires have seen a sharp recovery in their wealth from the March lows, riding a broader market rebound amid easing geopolitical tensions surrounding the US, Iran, and Israel conflict. However, rising crude oil prices continue to remain a concern.    Data analysed by Moneycontrol shows that among the biggest recoveries from the March lows are those of Gautam Adani, Ravi Jaipuria, Radhakishan Damani, Inder Jaisinghani, KP Singh, Lakshmi Mittal, Kumar Mangalam Birla, Savitri Jindal, and Samir Mehta.    Indian markets staged a strong comeback in April, with benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty gaining over 6 percent each. The broader markets saw an even sharper rally, with the BSE MidCap 150 index jumping 12.7 percent and the BSE SmallCap 250 index surging 18 percent.    Gautam Adani, founder of Adani Group, saw the biggest recovery, with his wealth jumping over 46 percent from its March low of $70 billion to $103 billion. The rebound was driven by a sharp run-up across group stocks. Adani Green Energy surged over 52 percent from its March low, followed by Adani Power which jumped 47 percent, Adani Energy Solutions up 44 percent, Adani Enterprises up 37 percent, and Adani Ports and SEZ along with Adani Total Gas advancing 26 percent each.    The second biggest recovery was seen in Ravi Jaipuria, founder and chairman of RJ Corp, whose wealth improved over 31 percent from its March low to $12.5 billion. The jump was driven by his Gurugram-based subsidiary Varun Beverages, whose stock climbed 34 percent from its March low.    Radhakishan Damani, who controls Avenue Supermarts, saw his wealth rise 24 percent to $19 billion from its March low of $15 billion. The DMart stock remained resilient even as markets tumbled during the conflict-driven selloff, gaining over 4 percent in February and 3 percent in March, before jumping 16 percent in April.    Inder Jaisinghani, chairman and managing director of Polycab — India's largest manufacturer of wires and cables — and KP Singh of DLF, the country's wealthiest property developer, saw their wealth jump nearly 17.4 percent and 16 percent respectively from their March lows.        Lakshmi Mittal, chairman of ArcelorMittal, the world's biggest steelmaker outside China, and Kumar Mangalam Birla, chairman of Aditya Birla Group, each saw their wealth recover 14 percent. Savitri Jindal, India's wealthiest woman and controller of OP Jindal Group, saw her wealth improve 13 percent. Samir Mehta, chairman of Torrent Group, and Murali Divi, founder and managing director of Divi's Laboratories, each saw their wealth improve 10 percent.    Among others, Rahul Bhatia, co-founder of IndiGo parent InterGlobe Aviation, Uday Kotak, former managing director of Kotak Mahindra Bank, and Sudhir Mehta, chairman of Torrent Group, each saw around 9 percent rise in wealth from the March lows. Vikram Lal, founder of Eicher Motors, Shapoor Mistry and family, and Cyrus Poonawalla, chairman of Serum Institute of India — the world's biggest vaccine manufacturer — saw around 8 percent rise in their wealth during the same period.    Azim Premji, founder of Wipro, Nusli Wadia, chairman of Britannia Industries, Sunil Mittal, chairman of Bharti Airtel, and Mukesh Ambani, chairman of Reliance Industries, saw their wealth rise 6 to 7 percent during the period.    Not all billionaires, however, shared in the recovery. Shiv Nadar, founder of HCL Technologies, saw his wealth erode 6 percent during the period, with his current wealth standing at $28.6 billion compared to $30.4 billion at the end of March. The decline came after HCL Technologies stock saw a sharp selloff following its March quarter earnings, weighed down by a weak revenue guidance of 1 to 4 percent growth for FY27 and a revenue miss in the fourth quarter of FY26.    Indian markets had witnessed a heavy selloff in March following the escalation of the conflict involving the US, Iran, and Israel, with crude oil surging past $100 per barrel. During this period, several global brokerages downgraded Indian markets and cut their Nifty targets amid expectations of slowing earnings. Some brokerages noted that while Indian market valuations corrected during this period, they were still not cheap enough to attract fresh buying interest from foreign investors.
